F.2 From the empirical noise distribution to independent noise

1.1.1/1.1.12/1.3.10

In the working regime of Section §1.1, positivity and proportional scaling give \mathbb{P}(N_{a}\geq 1)\to 1. The required bound on B_{a,t} is verified below.

1.1.1/1.1.12/1.3.11

Proposition 6 (paper: proposition (Proposition F.2 (Independent noise comparison).))

Fix a\in[K] and a finite grid \mathcal{T}. Assume the known positive logging probabilities in Assumption Assumption 1, the noise law in ((605)), the empirical moment conditions in ((606)), and 0\leq w_{a}\leq B_{h}<\infty. Assume that \mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)} and \mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)} are finite almost surely for every t\in\mathcal{T}. For every t\in\mathcal{T}, on \{N_{a}\geq 1\},

\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}=2\bar{\xi}_{a}B_{a,t}+\left(\overline{\xi_{a}^{2}}-\sigma_{\xi,a}^{2}\right)C_{w,a}. (280)

If \mathbb{P}(N_{a}\geq 1)\to 1 and \sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|B_{a,t}|=d^{o_{p}(1)} as d\to\infty, then

\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}|\xrightarrow{p}0. (281)

1.1.1/1.1.12/1.3.12\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}=2\bar{\xi}_{a}B_{a,t}+\left(\overline{\xi_{a}^{2}}-\sigma_{\xi,a}^{2}\right)C_{w,a}.(280)
1.1.1/1.1.12/1.3.13\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}|\xrightarrow{p}0.(281)
1.1.1/1.1.12/1.3.14

Proof.

On \{N_{a}\geq 1\}, conditional on \widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}, \pi_{N_{a}} is uniform on [N_{a}] and is independent of Z_{a}. Hence

\mathbb{E}[\xi_{\pi_{N_{a}},a}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}]=\bar{\xi}_{a},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\xi_{\pi_{N_{a}},a}^{2}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}]=\overline{\xi_{a}^{2}}. (282)

Expanding the two squared residuals therefore yields

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}

For the second identity, the cross term is zero because \xi_{a}^{\mathrm{new}} is centered and independent of (Z_{a},\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}). Subtracting the two identities proves ((280)).

We next verify the sufficient bound on B_{a,t} under the conditions of Section §1.1. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz and 0\leq w_{a}\leq B_{h} yield

\displaystyle|B_{a,t}|^{2}

Moreover,

m_{t}(Z_{a})^{2}\leq 2|\varphi_{a}^{\ast}(\beta_{a}^{\top}Z_{a})|^{2}+2|f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z_{a})|^{2}. (287)

The link term has finite deterministic expectation because \beta_{a}^{\top}Z_{a}\sim N(0,1) and \varphi_{a}^{\ast} has polynomial growth. For the prediction term, Lemma 1 gives

\mathbb{E}\left[|f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z_{a})|^{2}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[|f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z_{a})|^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}\right]. (288)

The right-hand side is uniformly d^{o_{p}(1)} on \mathcal{T} by Proposition 5. Thus

\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|B_{a,t}|=d^{o_{p}(1)}. (289)

Whether the bound on B_{a,t} is assumed directly or obtained above, the empirical moment conditions ((606)) give

\bar{\xi}_{a}=O_{p}(d^{-1/2}),\qquad\overline{\xi_{a}^{2}}-\sigma_{\xi,a}^{2}=o_{p}(1). (290)

Choose 0<\eta<1/2. Equations ((289)) and ((290)) give

|\bar{\xi}_{a}|\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|B_{a,t}|=O_{p}(d^{-1/2})\,O_{p}(d^{\eta})=O_{p}(d^{-1/2+\eta})=o_{p}(1). (291)

Finally, C_{w,a}\leq B_{h}, so on \{N_{a}\geq 1\}, ((280)) implies

\displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}|

The right-hand side is o_{p}(1). Since \mathbb{P}(N_{a}=0)\to 0, the claimed convergence holds regardless of the definitions on empty arms. ∎

Proposition 7 (paper: proposition (Proposition F.3 (Weighted averages of corrected predictions).))

Assume the conditions of Section §1.1, with fixed K,L,q,\mathcal{T}. For every a\in[K], t\in\mathcal{T}, and r\geq 1, on E_{\mathrm{cnt}},

\mathbb{E}_{a}^{(0)}|\widehat{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)}-M_{a}^{(t)}|^{r}\leq C_{t,r}(\varkappa_{\ast,a}\log d)^{C_{t,r}}d^{-1/C_{t,r}}. (303)

\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{a}^{(t)}(\Phi^{\mathrm{fit}})=\widehat{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)},\qquad\mathcal{O}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}(\Phi^{\mathrm{fit}})=\mathbb{E}\left[w_{a}(Z)f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z)\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}\right]. (297)

Appendix G Uniform Consistency and Model Selection

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.1.2

We combine the arm-wise risk comparisons to prove uniform consistency of the risk criterion over the fixed iterate grid. We then derive the oracle inequality for model selection and the resulting bound on policy value error.

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.2.1

G.1 Proof of Theorem 4.1

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.2.2

See Theorem 1

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.2.3

Proof.

Fix an arm a. By Proposition 4,

\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0. (305)

By Proposition 6,

\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0. (306)

Therefore

\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert\leq\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}\right\rvert+\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert, (307)

and the right-hand side is o_{p}(1). This proves the theorem. ∎

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.3.7\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g)(316)
1.1.1/1.1.13/1.3.8

Proof of Proposition 8.

Let \mathcal{H} denote either the trivial sigma-field or \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, let \tilde{g} be \mathcal{H}-measurable, and let (X,A,R) be an independent test draw. Since the logging policy is context independent,

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\tilde{g}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)

Conditional Cauchy–Schwarz yields

\displaystyle\left\lvert\mathcal{V}_{\tilde{g}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right\rvert

The first factor equals one because

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[w_{A}(X)\,|\,X,\mathcal{H}]

and the square of the second factor is

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\left(\tilde{g}(X,A)-g^{\ast}(X,A)\right)^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X)\left(\tilde{g}(X,a)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\right)^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]=\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(\tilde{g}).

This proves the value bound.

For the risk decomposition, write \varepsilon\coloneqq R-g^{\ast}(X,A) and \delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A)\coloneqq g^{\ast}(X,A)-\tilde{g}(X,A). Then, R-\tilde{g}(X,A)=\varepsilon+\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A), and expanding the square yields

\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(\tilde{g})

The cross term is zero, since iterated conditioning yields

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\varepsilon\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A)\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\delta_{\tilde{g}}(X,A)\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\,|\,X,A,\mathcal{H}]\,|\,\mathcal{H}\right]=0.

The first remaining term is \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g^{\ast}) and the second is \mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(\tilde{g}), proving the decomposition. Taking \mathcal{H} to be trivial gives the deterministic statement, while taking \mathcal{H}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}} gives its conditional out-of-sample version. ∎

□

Proof.

Set

\Delta_{a}\coloneqq\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}|. (332)

Let t_{a}^{\star} be the first minimizer of \mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)} on the fixed ordered grid \mathcal{T}. Since \hat{t}_{a} minimizes \widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)},

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(\hat{t}_{a})}

The definition of t_{a}^{\star} also gives the lower bound, so

0\leq\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(\hat{t}_{a})}-\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\leq 2\Delta_{a}. (336)

For every \epsilon>0, the fixed number of arms gives

\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{a\in[K]}\Delta_{a}>\epsilon\right)\leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\mathbb{P}(\Delta_{a}>\epsilon)\longrightarrow 0 (337)

by Theorem 1. Thus, \max_{a}\Delta_{a}=o_{p}(1).

We next identify the part of the arm-wise test risk that depends on the predictor. Write \delta_{a,t}(Z_{a})\coloneqq g^{\ast}(Z_{a},a)-g_{a,t}(Z_{a}). Since g_{a,t} is \widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}-measurable, Lemma 1 gives

\mathbb{E}\left[\nu(a\,|\,Z_{a})\delta_{a,t}(Z_{a})^{2}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\nu(a\,|\,Z_{a})\delta_{a,t}(Z_{a})^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}\right]=\mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a,t}). (318)

Since \mu(a)w_{a}(Z_{a})=\nu(a\,|\,Z_{a}),

\displaystyle\mu(a)\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}

where

C_{a}\coloneqq\mu(a)\mathbb{E}\left[w_{a}(Z_{a})(\xi_{a}^{\mathrm{new}})^{2}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}\right]=\sigma_{\xi,a}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\nu(a\,|\,Z_{a})]. (321)

Thus, C_{a} does not depend on t. The cross term is zero because \mathbb{E}[\xi_{a}^{\mathrm{new}}\,|\,Z_{a},\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a}]=0. Therefore

\mu(a)\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}=C_{a}+\mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a,t}),\qquad t\in\mathcal{T}. (322)

Substituting ((322)) into ((336)) and canceling C_{a} gives

0\leq\mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a,\hat{t}_{a}})-\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a,t})\leq 2\mu(a)\Delta_{a}. (323)

By Lemma 1, each arm-wise test risk has the same value when conditioned on \widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a} or on \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Therefore, for every \mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{K})\in\mathcal{T}^{K}, conditioning on the fresh logged action in the definition of \mathcal{R}_{\nu} gives

\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\mathbf{t}})=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\mu(a)\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t_{a})}\qquad\text{for every }\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K} (324)

so minimization over \mathcal{T}^{K} separates across arms:

\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\mathbf{t}})=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\mu(a)\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}. (325)

Consequently, ((336)) implies

\displaystyle 0

By Proposition 8, \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g)=\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g^{\ast})+\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g), where \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g^{\ast}) is constant in g. Subtracting this common term from the preceding oracle inequality gives

\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}})\leq\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\mathbf{t}})+o_{p}(1). (329)

Applying the value bound from the same proposition now yields

\displaystyle|\mathcal{V}_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)|^{2}

which proves all claims. ∎

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.18

The example satisfies the working assumptions: the reward link and activation are identity maps, the noise is zero, the importance weights are constant, and \sqrt{d}\,\|\beta\|_{\infty}=1 with bounded initializations. It concerns a fixed validation fraction; Appendix §1.4 examines two vanishing-fraction alternatives empirically.

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.2

With a fixed validation fraction, cross-validation estimates the test risk of models trained at a different limiting sample-to-dimension ratio. The following example shows that ten-fold cross-validation can correctly rank these models yet select a suboptimal iterate after full-data refitting.

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.3

Let F_{1},\ldots,F_{10} partition [m] independently of the observations, with |F_{j}|=m/10+o(m). Write g_{a,t}^{(-j)} for the arm-a model trained on \mathcal{I}_{a}\setminus F_{j}, using the same initialization and learning rates as the full-data model g_{a,t}. On \mathcal{T}=\{0,1\}, define

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.4\widehat{\mathcal{E}}^{\rm CV}_{a}(t)\coloneqq\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{j=1}^{10}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}\cap F_{j}}\{R_{i}-g_{a,t}^{(-j)}(X_{i})\}^{2},\qquad\hat{t}_{a}^{\rm CV}\in\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\widehat{\mathcal{E}}^{\rm CV}_{a}(t).(346)
1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.5

The importance weights equal one in the example below. Let t_{a}^{\star}\in\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a,t}) be the full-data risk minimizer, and set \hat{\mathbf{t}}^{\rm CV}=(\hat{t}_{1}^{\rm CV},\ldots,\hat{t}_{K}^{\rm CV}). Break ties toward t=0 and use any measurable convention when a required arm count is zero; the latter event has probability tending to zero.

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.6

Proposition 9 (paper: proposition (Proposition G.2 (Suboptimal stopping after cross-validation).))

Let X_{i}\overset{\rm iid}{\sim}N(0,I_{d}), let K\geq 2 be fixed, and assume context-independent logging with \mu(a)=\nu(a\mid x)=1/K and m/d\to K. Take noiseless rewards R_{i}=g^{\ast}(X_{i},A_{i})=\beta^{\top}X_{i}, where \beta=d^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^{\top}. For every full-data and fold-complement fit, use the depth-two, width-one network with identity activation, initialization W_{a,1}^{(0)}=0, W_{a,2}^{(0)}=1, and first-layer step size \eta=39/40. The second-layer step size may be any fixed positive number satisfying Assumption Assumption 4. Then, as d\to\infty,

\mathbb{P}\bigl(\hat{t}_{a}^{\rm CV}=0,\ t_{a}^{\star}=1\text{ for every }a\in[K]\bigr)\longrightarrow 1, (347)

and the full-data model selected by CV has a nonvanishing excess prediction risk over the best candidate iterates:

\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}^{\rm CV}})-\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\{0,1\}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\mathbf{t}})\xrightarrow{p}\frac{39}{800}. (348)

1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.7\mathbb{P}\bigl(\hat{t}_{a}^{\rm CV}=0,\ t_{a}^{\star}=1\text{ for every }a\in[K]\bigr)\longrightarrow 1,(347)
1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.8\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}^{\rm CV}})-\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\{0,1\}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\mathbf{t}})\xrightarrow{p}\frac{39}{800}.(348)
1.1.1/1.1.13/1.5.9

Proof.

For a training set of n observations in an arm, let S_{n}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}X_{i}^{\top}. The deeper-layer gradient is zero at initialization, and one simultaneous gradient-descent update yields g_{1}(x)=\eta x^{\top}S_{n}\beta. For an independent Z\sim N(0,I_{d}), the initialization has prediction risk \|\beta\|^{2}=1, while the first iterate has conditional prediction risk

\displaystyle r_{n} (338)

To verify the limit, Gaussian rotational invariance allows us to take \beta=e_{1}. Write z_{i}=X_{i1} and s_{n}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}z_{i}^{2}\to_{p}1. Conditional on (z_{i})_{i=1}^{n}, the other coordinates of S_{n}\beta are independent N(0,s_{n}/n) variables. Thus

r_{n}\ \overset{\rm d}{=}\ (\eta s_{n}-1)^{2}+\eta^{2}\frac{s_{n}}{n}U_{d-1},\qquad U_{d-1}\sim\chi^{2}_{d-1}\text{ independent of }s_{n}. (340)

Since U_{d-1}/d\to_{p}1, this proves ((338)). The calculation also applies conditional on the action labels and fold partition when the training count is random and n/d\to_{p}\alpha.

Let v_{a,j}=|\mathcal{I}_{a}\cap F_{j}| and n_{a,-j}=N_{a}-v_{a,j}. Uniform logging and m/d\to K give, jointly over the fixed numbers of arms and folds,

\frac{N_{a}}{d}\xrightarrow{p}1,\qquad\frac{v_{a,j}}{d}\xrightarrow{p}\frac{1}{10},\qquad\frac{n_{a,-j}}{d}\xrightarrow{p}\frac{9}{10}. (341)

Write r_{a,-j} for the conditional prediction risk of g_{a,1}^{(-j)}. By ((338)), r_{a,-j}\to_{p}r(9/10). Conditional on the action labels, fold partition, and training data outside fold j, the validation residuals are independent N(0,r_{a,-j}) variables. Their mean square therefore has conditional mean r_{a,-j} and variance 2r_{a,-j}^{2}/v_{a,j}=o_{p}(1). Conditional Chebyshev’s inequality and a finite union over arms and folds yield

\frac{1}{v_{a,j}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}\cap F_{j}}\{R_{i}-g_{a,1}^{(-j)}(X_{i})\}^{2}=r_{a,-j}+o_{p}(1). (342)

Since the CV criterion averages these fold errors with weights v_{a,j}/N_{a}, we obtain, for every arm,

\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{E}}^{\rm CV}_{a}(0)

The strict inequalities imply the stated selection event. On that event, the excess prediction risk equals

\frac{1}{K}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\{1-K\mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a,1})\}\xrightarrow{p}1-\frac{761}{800}=\frac{39}{800}. (345)

This proves both conclusions. ∎

□

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.1.1

Appendix H Value Estimation Without Sample Splitting and Consequences

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.1.10\displaystyle\max_{a\neq b}\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\overline{M}_{a,b}^{(t)}-M_{b}^{(t)}|(349)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.1.100\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})-\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})=\left[\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right]-\left[\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(\nu)\right]-\left[\mathcal{V}_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right].(350)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.1.11\displaystyle\max_{a\in[K]}\left|\frac{N_{a}}{m}-\mu(a)\right|(351)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.1.12\displaystyle\max_{a\in[K]}|\overline{R}_{a}-R_{a}^{\star}|(352)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.1.13\displaystyle\max_{a\in[K]}\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|M_{a}^{(t)}|(353)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.1.14

Proof.

The diagonal fitted-value bound follows from Proposition 7 and a finite union over the arms. For a\neq b, let

\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{b}\coloneqq\sigma(\mathcal{I}_{b},X_{\mathcal{I}_{b}},R_{\mathcal{I}_{b}},W_{b}^{(0)}), (354)

and let

\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}\coloneqq\sigma(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m},X_{\mathcal{I}_{b}},R_{\mathcal{I}_{b}},W_{b}^{(0)}). (355)

The count event E_{\mathrm{cnt}} is measurable with respect to \widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}. For the off-diagonal comparison, work on this event, so N_{a}\geq 1. Conditional on \widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}, the arm-b predictor is fixed, while \{X_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}\} are i.i.d. N(0,I_{d}) and independent of that predictor. Because Z is independent of \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, the definition of M_{b}^{(t)} is unchanged if \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}} is replaced by \widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{b}; hence, M_{b}^{(t)} is \widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}-measurable. It follows that the variables Y_{i,b}^{(t)}\coloneqq w_{b}(X_{i})f_{W_{b}^{(t)}}(X_{i}), i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}, are conditionally i.i.d. with mean M_{b}^{(t)}. The same conditioning argument shows that the second moment of w_{b}(Z)f_{W_{b}^{(t)}}(Z) agrees under \widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b} and \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Boundedness of w_{b} and Proposition 5 therefore give

\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}[|Y_{i,b}^{(t)}|^{2}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}]=d^{o_{p}(1)}. (356)

Therefore,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[|\overline{M}_{a,b}^{(t)}-M_{b}^{(t)}|^{2}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}\right]

uniformly over the fixed grid. For every \epsilon>0, conditional Chebyshev’s inequality and measurability of E_{\mathrm{cnt}} give

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|\overline{M}_{a,b}^{(t)}-M_{b}^{(t)}|>\epsilon\right)\leq\mathbb{P}(E_{\mathrm{cnt}}^{c})+\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}_{E_{\mathrm{cnt}}}\min\left\{1,\frac{\mathbb{E}[|Y_{i,b}^{(t)}|^{2}\,|\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{a,b}]}{N_{a}\epsilon^{2}}\right\}\right].

The integrand is bounded by one and, by ((358)), converges to zero in probability. Its expectation therefore converges to zero. Since \mathbb{P}(E_{\mathrm{cnt}}^{c})\to 0, a finite union over (a,b,t) proves the second claim.

For the count bound, N_{a}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,\mu(a)), so

\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{N_{a}}{m}\right]=\mu(a),\qquad\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{N_{a}}{m}\right)=\frac{\mu(a)\{1-\mu(a)\}}{m}. (360)

For every M>0, Chebyshev’s inequality and a union bound give

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sqrt{d}\max_{a}|N_{a}/m-\mu(a)|>M\right)

where C is uniform in d because m\asymp d and K is fixed. Letting M\to\infty proves the third claim.

For the reward-average comparison, continue to work on E_{\mathrm{cnt}}. Decompose

\displaystyle\overline{R}_{a}-R_{a}^{\star}

For the first term, conditional on the action labels, independence and the link moment bound give

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}\{w_{a}(X_{i})g^{\ast}(X_{i},a)-R_{a}^{\star}\}\right|^{2}\,|\,A_{1:m}\right]=\frac{\operatorname{Var}\{w_{a}(X)g^{\ast}(X,a)\}}{N_{a}}\leq\frac{C}{N_{a}}\leq\frac{C}{c_{-}d}

on E_{\mathrm{cnt}}. Hence, this term is O_{p}(d^{-1/2}). The second term is also O_{p}(d^{-1/2}) by ((606)) and \mathbb{E}[w_{a}(X)]\leq B_{h}. For the last term, condition additionally on the realized noises and write

S_{a}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}\{w_{a}(X_{i})-\mathbb{E}[w_{a}(X)]\}\varepsilon_{i}. (364)

The contexts are conditionally independent, so

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[S_{a}\,|\,A_{1:m},\varepsilon_{1:m}]

on E_{\mathrm{cnt}}. Conditional Chebyshev’s inequality yields, for \epsilon>0,

\mathbb{P}(|S_{a}|>\epsilon)\leq\mathbb{P}(E_{\mathrm{cnt}}^{c})+\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}_{E_{\mathrm{cnt}}}\min\left\{1,\frac{B_{h}^{2}\varkappa_{\ast,a}^{2}}{c_{-}d\epsilon^{2}}\right\}\right]\longrightarrow 0. (368)

As above, the integrand is bounded by one and converges to zero in probability, so its expectation converges to zero. Combining the three terms and taking a finite union over the arms proves the fourth claim.

Under the sub-Gaussian noise condition in Assumption 2, \operatorname{Var}(w_{a}(X)R\,|\,A=a) is uniformly bounded. Conditional on \mathcal{I}_{a}, the weighted rewards are i.i.d. with mean R_{a}^{\star} and variance bounded by a constant. Thus, on E_{\mathrm{cnt}},

\mathbb{E}[|\overline{R}_{a}-R_{a}^{\star}|^{2}\,|\,A_{1:m}]=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(w_{a}(X)R\,|\,A=a)}{N_{a}}\leq\frac{C}{c_{-}d}. (369)

For M>0, conditional Chebyshev’s inequality and a union bound yield

\mathbb{P}\left(\sqrt{d}\max_{a}|\overline{R}_{a}-R_{a}^{\star}|>M\right)\leq\mathbb{P}(E_{\mathrm{cnt}}^{c})+\frac{KC}{c_{-}M^{2}}. (370)

Taking d\to\infty and then M\to\infty proves the sharper bound.

Finally, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz yields

\displaystyle|M_{a}^{(t)}|^{2}

By Lemma 1, the same conditional prediction-moment bound holds with conditioning on \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. The fixed-grid bound in Proposition 5, followed by a finite union over arms, proves the last claim. ∎

We first recall the empirical-process condition used in classical analyses of DR estimators. We then examine whether this condition holds over the neural-network class considered here and derive the estimation error along the fitted gradient-descent trajectory. Let P_{m,d} be the empirical measure of the training sample. For a function that depends on the fitted model, P_{d} denotes expectation over an independent observation Q=(X,A,R), conditional on \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Write \mathbb{G}_{m,d}=\sqrt{m}(P_{m,d}-P_{d}). Consider the DR estimator obtained by substituting the fitted networks g_{\mathbf{t}} into \psi_{g} and averaging over their training sample, without the Onsager correction:

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.20

Remark 1 (paper: remark (Remark H.5.))

The predictors in Proposition 10 are represented by the permitted network with depth two, width one, and identity activation: take W_{1}=\theta and W_{2}=1. The architecture and scaling assumptions therefore do not imply local stochastic equicontinuity over the entire predictor class.

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.21

We now analyze the DR estimator formed from the fitted gradient-descent iterates. Order the arm-a observations as \mathcal{I}_{a}=\{i_{a,1},\ldots,i_{a,N_{a}}\}, and define the weighted average of the uncorrected predictions on that arm’s training observations by

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.22\widetilde{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}w_{a}(X_{i})G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}(X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)}).(423)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.23

Write V_{a}^{(t)}\coloneqq(V_{a,\alpha}^{(t)})_{\alpha\in[2:L]} for the deeper-layer quantities in the state evolution, and define the state-evolution approximation to this training-sample average by

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.27

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.28M_{a}^{(t)}=\mathbb{E}\left[w_{a}(Z)f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z)\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{m},W_{a}^{(0)}\right](426)

is the expected weighted prediction at an independent context, conditional on the fitted model. Thus, D_{a,d}(t) is the difference between the state-evolution approximation to the training-sample average and the corresponding conditional expectation at an independent context. Both quantities can depend on d and the training data; neither is assumed to have a limit. The weighted sum \mathfrak{b}_{d}(\mathbf{t}) will describe the leading estimation error of DR on the training sample.

Lemma 7 (paper: lemma (Lemma H.6 (Uncorrected predictions on training observations).))

Under the conditions of Section §1.1, with fixed K,L,q,\mathcal{T}, for every arm a\in[K], as d\to\infty,

\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left|\widetilde{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)}-M_{a,d}^{\mathrm{tr},(t)}\right|\xrightarrow{p}0. (428)

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.31\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left|\widetilde{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)}-M_{a,d}^{\mathrm{tr},(t)}\right|\xrightarrow{p}0.(428)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.32

Proof.

Fix a and condition as in Proposition 1. In the local arm-wise notation used in the comparison proof, the uncorrected first-layer state is \hat{u}_{k}^{(t+1)}=X_{i_{a,k}}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)}. The gradient-descent comparison in Lemma 4, at horizon t+1, gives

N_{a}^{-1/2}\|\hat{u}^{(t+1)}-u^{(t+1)}\|_{F}=o_{p}(1),\qquad\max_{\alpha\in[2:L]}\|W_{a,\alpha}^{(t)}-V_{a,\alpha}^{(t)}\|_{\infty}=o_{p}(1), (429)

with the stated conditional polynomial-moment rates. By HI25 Proposition -(1)(2), there is a random \mathcal{P}_{a,t}, whose fixed conditional moments are bounded by a polynomial in \varkappa_{\ast,a}\log d, such that

\displaystyle N_{a}^{-1/2}\left\|G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}(\hat{u}^{(t+1)})-G_{V_{a}^{(t)}}(u^{(t+1)})\right\|_{2}\leq\mathcal{P}_{a,t}\left\{N_{a}^{-1/2}\|\hat{u}^{(t+1)}-u^{(t+1)}\|_{F}+\max_{\alpha\in[2:L]}\|W_{a,\alpha}^{(t)}-V_{a,\alpha}^{(t)}\|_{\infty}\right\}.

Since |h_{a}|\leq B_{h}, Cauchy–Schwarz yields

\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{a}}h_{a}(\Upsilon^{\top}X_{i_{a,k}})\left\{G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}(\hat{u}_{k}^{(t+1)})-G_{V_{a}^{(t)}}(u_{k}^{(t+1)})\right\}\right|

By the bounded Lipschitz property of h_{a} and the forward-map derivative bounds, the test function

\vartheta_{a,t}(z^{([0:t+1])})=h_{a}\bigl((z^{(0)})^{\mathrm{idx}}\bigr)G_{V_{a}^{(t)}}\bigl((z^{(t+1)})^{\mathrm{aux}}\bigr) (433)

is, conditionally on \mathcal{G}_{a}, pseudo-Lipschitz of order two, with pseudo-Lipschitz constant bounded by

C_{t}\left\{1+\max_{\alpha\in[2:L]}\|V_{a,\alpha}^{(t)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\right\}^{C_{t}}. (434)

After conditioning on \mathcal{G}_{a}, this constant is deterministic. Apply item (30) of Proposition 2 at horizon t+1 with this constant. The resulting bound is polynomial in the displayed constant. The conditional moment bounds in Lemma 5, together with ((609)), therefore give the comparison with the target in ((424)):

\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{a}}h_{a}(\Upsilon^{\top}X_{i_{a,k}})G_{V_{a}^{(t)}}(u_{k}^{(t+1)})-M_{a,d}^{\mathrm{tr},(t)}=o_{p}(1). (435)

Combining this with the preceding comparison between the fitted and auxiliary predictions, and taking a finite union over t\in\mathcal{T}, proves the claim. ∎

□

Proposition 11 (paper: proposition (Proposition H.7 (Error of the DR estimator without sample splitting).))

Assume the conditions of Section §1.1, with fixed K,L,q,\mathcal{T}. Let \mathfrak{b}_{d} be defined by ((425)). For every \mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}, the estimators in ((427)) and ((556)) satisfy the exact identity

\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\mathbf{t})-\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})=-\sum_{a=1}^{K}\frac{N_{a}}{m}\{1-\mu(a)\}\left[\widetilde{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t_{a})}-\widehat{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t_{a})}\right].

Moreover,

\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left|\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}(\nu)-\mathfrak{b}_{d}(\mathbf{t})\right|\xrightarrow{p}0. (437)

Consequently, for any \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}-measurable choice \widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}, the estimator \widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d}) is consistent for \mathcal{V}(\nu) if and only if \mathfrak{b}_{d}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d})\xrightarrow{p}0. In particular, it is inconsistent whenever there is an \epsilon>0 such that

\limsup_{d\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(|\mathfrak{b}_{d}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d})|>\epsilon\right)>0. (438)

Proof.

For each observation i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}, \widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}} and \widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}} use the same reward and the same predictions for arms b\neq a. Their summands differ by -\{1-\mu(a)\}w_{a}(X_{i}) times the difference between the uncorrected and corrected predictions for arm a. Summing these differences gives ((436)).

By Lemma 7 and Proposition 7, uniformly on the fixed grid,

\widetilde{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)}-\widehat{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)}=D_{a,d}(t)+o_{p}(1). (439)

For the average of the uncorrected predictions, boundedness of h_{a} and Cauchy–Schwarz give

|\widetilde{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)}|\leq B_{h}\left\{\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}|f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(X_{i})|^{2}\right\}^{1/2}. (440)

The deterministic forward-map bounds and the normalized GD-state moment bounds make the right-hand side d^{o_{p}(1)}, uniformly on the fixed grid. The same argument with \widehat{U}_{a}^{(t)} and Lemma 5 gives \sup_{t}|\widehat{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t)}|=d^{o_{p}(1)}. Thus, the error from replacing N_{a}/m by \mu(a) in ((436)) is bounded by

\displaystyle\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left|\sum_{a=1}^{K}\left\{\frac{N_{a}}{m}-\mu(a)\right\}(1-\mu(a))\{\widetilde{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t_{a})}-\widehat{M}_{a,\mathrm{diag}}^{(t_{a})}\}\right|

Combining this bound with the preceding uniform comparison gives

\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left|\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\mathbf{t})-\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathfrak{b}_{d}(\mathbf{t})\right|\xrightarrow{p}0. (445)

The ADR part of Theorem 3 proves ((437)). Evaluating the uniform statement at \widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d} proves the final claim. ∎

Corollary 2 (paper: corollary (Corollary H.8 (Non-tightness of the empirical-process term).))

Assume the conditions of Proposition 11. Let \widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d}\in\mathcal{T}^{K} be \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}-measurable and set H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}=\psi_{g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d}}}-\psi_{g^{\ast}}. Then

\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}=\mathfrak{b}_{d}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d})+o_{p}(1). (446)

If the separation condition in Proposition 11 holds, then \mathbb{G}_{m,d}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d} is not tight. In particular, no classes \mathcal{H}_{d} can both contain H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d} with probability tending to one and satisfy

\sup_{H\in\mathcal{H}_{d}}|\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H|=O_{p}(1) (447)

uniformly in d.

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.53\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}=\mathfrak{b}_{d}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d})+o_{p}(1).(446)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.54\sup_{H\in\mathcal{H}_{d}}|\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H|=O_{p}(1)(447)
1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.55

Proof.

Pathwise, P_{d}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}=0, so

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}

By Proposition 11, \widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d})-\mathcal{V}(\nu) is \mathfrak{b}_{d}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d})+o_{p}(1). To control the empirical average that uses g^{\ast}, work on E_{\mathrm{cnt}} and write

\displaystyle P_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu)

The first term is O_{p}(d^{-1/2}) by the uniformly bounded signal second moment. Each weighted noise average in the second term is o_{p}(1) by the reward-average argument in Lemma 6. Since \mathbb{P}(E_{\mathrm{cnt}}^{c})\to 0, it follows that P_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu)=o_{p}(1), proving ((446)). Under the separation condition, there exist \epsilon,\delta>0 and a subsequence d_{j} such that

\mathbb{P}(|\mathfrak{b}_{d_{j}}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d_{j}})|>\epsilon)>\delta. (451)

Let

r_{d}\coloneqq m^{-1/2}\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}-\mathfrak{b}_{d}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d})=o_{p}(1). (452)

For every fixed M>0, eventually M<\epsilon\sqrt{m}/2 along this subsequence, and

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|\mathbb{G}_{m,d_{j}}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d_{j}},d_{j}}|>M\right)

This contradicts tightness. If a class \mathcal{H}_{d} contains the fitted score error with probability tending to one, then

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|\mathbb{G}_{m,d}H_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}_{d},d}|>M\right)

Thus, the stated uniform class bound would imply tightness and cannot hold. ∎

1.1.1/1.1.14/1.2.66

Proof.

Work on E_{\mathrm{cnt}}; its complement has probability tending to zero. Since f_{W_{a}^{(0)}}=0, W_{a,1}^{(0)}=0, and W_{a,2}^{(0)}=1, the two gradients are

\displaystyle\nabla_{W_{a,1}}\mathcal{L}_{a}(W_{a}^{(0)})

The simultaneous update therefore gives

W_{a,1}^{(1)}=\eta c\overline{X}_{a},\qquad W_{a,2}^{(1)}=1,\qquad g_{a,1}(x)=\eta c\,x^{\top}\overline{X}_{a}. (458)

Since w_{a}=1 and \mathcal{V}(\nu)=c, direct substitution into ((427)) gives

\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}-c=\eta c\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\mu(a)\overline{X}^{\top}\overline{X}_{a}-\sum_{a=1}^{K}\frac{N_{a}}{m}\|\overline{X}_{a}\|_{2}^{2}\right],\qquad\overline{X}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i}. (459)

Conditional on the action labels,

\frac{N_{a}}{m}\|\overline{X}_{a}\|_{2}^{2}\overset{d}{=}\frac{\chi_{d,a}^{2}}{m}\xrightarrow{p}\frac{1}{\phi}. (460)

Also,

\overline{X}^{\top}\overline{X}_{a}=\frac{N_{a}}{m}\|\overline{X}_{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\sum_{b\neq a}\frac{N_{b}}{m}\overline{X}_{b}^{\top}\overline{X}_{a}\xrightarrow{p}\frac{1}{\phi}, (461)

because, for a\neq b, conditional independence gives

\mathbb{E}[\overline{X}_{b}^{\top}\overline{X}_{a}\mid A_{1:m}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[(\overline{X}_{b}^{\top}\overline{X}_{a})^{2}\mid A_{1:m}]=\frac{d}{N_{a}N_{b}}=O(d^{-1}) (462)

on E_{\mathrm{cnt}}. Thus, every cross-arm inner product is o_{p}(1). The two sums in the expression for \widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}-c therefore converge to 1/\phi and K/\phi, respectively. Since \mathbb{P}(E_{\mathrm{cnt}}^{c})\to 0, the claimed limit follows. The example uses a constant smooth reward link, zero noise, constant importance weights, a smooth identity activation, and deterministic sample-independent initialization, so it satisfies the working assumptions. By Proposition 11, this limit also implies

\mathfrak{b}_{d}(1,\ldots,1)\xrightarrow{p}-\frac{\eta c(K-1)}{\phi}, (463)

so the separation condition holds. ∎

Remark 2 (paper: remark (Remark H.3 (Donsker conditions and cross-fitting).))

When the data distribution P is fixed, asymptotic stochastic equicontinuity yields \mathbb{G}_{m}H_{\widehat{g}}=o_{p}(1) if, with probability tending to one, H_{\widehat{g}} belongs to a fixed P-Donsker class and \|H_{\widehat{g}}\|_{P,2}=o_{p}(1). Cross-fitting evaluates each fitted reward model on observations excluded from its training sample. For each fold, conditional on its fitted model, the evaluation observations are independent with law P. With a fixed number of folds, conditional Chebyshev’s inequality therefore makes the cross-fitted empirical-process term o_{p}(1) when each fitted score error converges to zero in L^{2}(P), without a Donsker condition [[4]]. A fixed iterate grid gives finitely many models for each realized training sample. It does not put those models in a fixed Donsker class: as the data vary, each iterate ranges over a class whose input dimension grows with d.

Remark 3 (paper: remark (Remark H.9 (Asymptotic linearity and inference).))

Define the DR estimator that uses the true reward function by

\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{or}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\psi_{g^{\ast}}(Q_{i}). (464)

Let \Delta_{i,a}=\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{t}}(X_{i},a)-g^{\ast}(X_{i},a) be the adjusted prediction error for observation i and arm a. Then

\sqrt{m}\{\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})-\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{or}}\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\mid X_{i})\Delta_{i,a}-w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})\Delta_{i,A_{i}}\right]. (465)

To obtain the asymptotic linear expansion

\sqrt{m}\{\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}})-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\{\psi_{g^{\ast}}(Q_{i})-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\}+o_{p}(1), (466)

the preceding prediction-error sum, evaluated at \mathbf{t}=\widehat{\mathbf{t}}, must be o_{p}(1). The consistency results prove only that it is o_{p}(\sqrt{m}).

Sufficient conditions for the expansion are

\sqrt{m}\{\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}})-\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{or}}\}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}H_{g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}},d}(Q_{i}^{\prime})=o_{p}(1), (467)

together with \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{var}}(g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}})=o_{p}(1). Here \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{var}} is the conditional variance of the score error in Proposition 12, and Q_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,Q_{m}^{\prime} are i.i.d. observations from the logged-data law, independent of \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Write the independent sum as

S_{m}^{\prime}\coloneqq\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}H_{g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}},d}(Q_{i}^{\prime}). (468)

Conditional independence and Proposition 12 give

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[S_{m}^{\prime}\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}]

Consequently, for every \epsilon>0,

\mathbb{P}(|S_{m}^{\prime}|>\epsilon)\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\min\left\{1,\epsilon^{-2}\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{var}}(g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}})\right\}\right]\longrightarrow 0 (472)

when \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{var}}(g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}})=o_{p}(1). The assumed comparison then gives \sqrt{m}(\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\widehat{\mathbf{t}})-\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{or}})=S_{m}^{\prime}+o_{p}(1)=o_{p}(1). By the selection guarantee and Proposition 12, the variance condition follows if

\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\mathbf{t}})=o_{p}(1). (473)

Our assumptions permit prediction error that does not converge to zero, and the comparisons proved above do not establish the required o_{p}(1) remainder at the \sqrt{m} scale.

In the nonparametric model with known logging probabilities and unrestricted context and reward distributions, \psi_{g^{\ast}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu) is the efficient influence function [[17]]. The Gaussian single-index model considered here imposes additional restrictions, so its efficiency bound requires a separate calculation. The notation \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2} in Corollary 3 denotes the variance of \psi_{g^{\ast}}.

The state-evolution results in this paper assume that the arm-wise aspect ratios stay bounded above and away from zero, with fixed network width and training horizon. Extending these results to m/d\to\infty, growing width, or a growing training horizon requires new bounds that are uniform in the corresponding parameters.

We next use the exact noise identity ((280)). Since \varkappa_{\ast,a} contains the maximum realized arm-wise noise, ((536)) with s=2,4 implies

Appendix J Additional Experiments and Implementation Details

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.10.1

J.9 Numerical reference values and uncertainty

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.10.2

Reference test risks are conditional on the fitted models. For Gaussian contexts, we integrate the joint Gaussian vector of signal and policy indices and fitted first-layer projections using two independent scrambled Sobol rules with antithetic points, each containing 2^{14} points. For non-Gaussian contexts, we average two independent Monte Carlo estimates, each using 16,384 draws and their negatives from the specified context law. The reward-noise contribution is integrated analytically. All reference draws are independent of the logged data and are used only to assess the procedures; they do not enter fitting, selection, or the value estimators.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.10.3

The true policy value is computed by Gaussian integration, a finite sum over binomial sign counts for Rademacher contexts, or numerical inversion of the signal sums’ characteristic functions for standardized t_{5} contexts. Errors of DM, ADM, and cross-arm DM are measured against the average of the two independent numerical references for each fitted model’s value.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.10.4

For normalized value MSE, we compute \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}=\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{g^{\ast}}(X,A,R)\} by Gaussian integration and use the true-reward score average \widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{or}}=m^{-1}\sum_{i}\psi_{g^{\ast}}(Q_{i}) as a control variate. Specifically, we average

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.10.51+\frac{m}{\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}}\left\{(\widehat{\mathcal{V}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu))^{2}-(\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{or}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu))^{2}\right\}(540)
1.1.1/1.1.16/1.10.6

over datasets; the control squared error has mean \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}/m.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.10.7

All pointwise 95\% intervals use Student t quantiles across independent logged datasets. They describe Monte Carlo uncertainty in performance, rather than uncertainty in policy value from a single dataset. RMSE intervals take square roots of the MSE limits after truncating the lower limit at zero. Comparisons use within-dataset differences; in the target-policy experiment, averages over nonuniform policies are also formed within each dataset before computing intervals.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.11.1

J.10 Value estimation as sample size outgrows dimension

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.11.2

We compare ADR, DR with ten-fold cross-fitting (CF10), inverse propensity scoring (IPS), and self-normalized IPS (SNIPS) as the number of observations increases relative to the context dimension. We use the two-arm model above and train every reward network with \eta=1 over candidate iterations \{0,\ldots,30\}. Both corrected-stopping and inner-validation CF10 use the protocols in Appendix §1.3; each evaluation fold is excluded from fitting and selection. We first fix d=256 and increase m\in\{512,2048,8192,32768\}. We also increase both dimension and sample-to-dimension ratio along (d,m)\in\{(256,2048),(512,8192),(1024,32768)\}. Each setting uses 200 independent datasets, except those with m=32768, which use 100.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.11.3

We report normalized mean squared error, m\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\mathcal{V}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu))^{2}]/\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}, where \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}=\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{g^{\ast}}(X,A,R)\}. The normalization \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}/m is the exact MSE of DR using the true reward function, whose normalized MSE is therefore one for every (d,m). At a fixed data law, \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2} is also the classical semiparametric variance bound for known logging and otherwise unrestricted context and reward distributions. We use it here as an oracle reference. We estimate normalized MSE using the control-variate calculation in Appendix §1.10.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.11.4

Figure Figure 1 shows ADR and both CF10 procedures approaching normalized MSE one as sample size outgrows dimension. At (d,m)=(1024,32768), ADR and corrected-stopping CF10 give 1.000 and 1.013, respectively. At both endpoints with m=32768, paired ADR-minus-corrected-CF10 intervals contain zero, while ADR’s MSE is lower than IPS and SNIPS with paired intervals below zero.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.12.1

J.11 Computational cost

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.12.2

ADR requires one full-data training trajectory per arm. Its response recursion adds O(N_{a}q^{3}T^{3}) operations and O(N_{a}T^{2}q^{2}) storage (Appendix §1.1). Corrected-stopping CF10 repeats this calculation on ten training complements. Table Table 5 shows that ADR is 5.5–8.9 times faster in the three benchmark settings. CV and inner-validation CF10 are faster in the smallest setting, while ADR is faster in the larger two.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.12.3

Both tables report median wall time over five shared datasets per setting, using the two-arm Gaussian model and training settings above, with \eta=2 when m=2d and \eta=1 at m=32768. Each measurement includes training, selection, refitting where required, and final value estimation; common data generation and reference integration are excluded. Runs use one numerical thread, with a separate warm-up excluded. The studies were conducted on different CPUs, so comparisons use the controls within each table.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.12.5

The single holdouts in Table Table 6 are faster than ADR. Together with Appendix §1.4, this identifies the trade-off: the correction improves risk estimation and stopping selection, while a single holdout costs less. The CV and holdout timings include full-data refitting and raw DR scoring; these procedures compare selection costs, since refitting alone does not correct same-sample DR bias.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.2.1

J.1 Synthetic data and network training

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.2.2

Unless stated otherwise, the Gaussian experiments use independent observations with X_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), A_{i}\sim\operatorname{Unif}([K]), and \varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.8^{2}), where the contexts, actions, and noises are mutually independent. The rewards are

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.2.3R_{i}=\varphi_{A_{i}}^{\ast}(\beta_{A_{i}}^{\top}X_{i})+\varepsilon_{i}.(541)
1.1.1/1.1.16/1.2.4

The two-arm baseline uses \varphi_{1}^{\ast}(y)=\tanh(y), \varphi_{2}^{\ast}(y)=\tanh(2y), and the logistic target policy \nu(1\mid x)=\sigma(2\beta_{1}^{\top}x), where \sigma(u)=(1+e^{-u})^{-1}. The signal directions are fixed, dense, and orthonormal. Other reward links and policies are specified below.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.2.5

For each arm, we train the network in Appendix §1.1 with sigmoid activation, depth L=2, and width q=5. First-layer entries are initialized independently from \mathcal{N}(0,1/d) and deeper-layer entries from \mathcal{N}(0,1/q), with columns 2,\ldots,q of the output matrix set to zero. Initial weights are fixed across datasets and shared by all procedures and folds. Every layer is updated by full-batch gradient descent on the unweighted loss \mathcal{L}_{a}, normalized by its arm-specific training count except in the leave-one-out diagnostic below. Candidate times are \mathcal{T}=\{0,\ldots,30\}. We use \eta=2 unless stated otherwise; the increasing-ratio experiment uses \eta=1 for every method.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.1

J.2 Stopping rules and comparison estimators

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.10

We also evaluate each arm’s selected predictor on contexts logged under other arms, without changing its training sample or stopping time:

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.11\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{cross}}=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\frac{1}{m-N_{a}}\sum_{i\notin\mathcal{I}_{a}}\nu(a\mid X_{i})f_{W_{a}^{(\hat{t}_{a})}}(X_{i}).(542)
1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.12

Here \hat{t}_{a} is selected by the corrected criterion using only arm-a data. Under context-independent logging, conditional on the action labels, the other arms’ contexts are independent of this fitted predictor; this is the off-diagonal independence argument in Lemma Lemma 6. The denominator is the actual number m-N_{a} of evaluation contexts. Like DM and ADM in this comparison, cross-arm DM targets the fitted-model value \mathcal{V}_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu), rather than the true policy value.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.13

Figure Figure 8 compares these estimators on the same 200 datasets and selected models per dimension. ADM reduces MSE relative to cross-arm DM by 50.7\%–57.4\%; all five paired pointwise 95\% intervals favor ADM. Both estimators’ bias intervals contain zero in every setting. The gain is therefore in precision for the fitted-model value.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.2

For a full-data model, the proposed stopping rule minimizes ((557)) separately for each arm. We compare it with the rule that minimizes the criterion obtained by replacing the corrected predictions with f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(X_{i}), and with ten-fold cross-validation. In the experiment with several target policies, we also minimize the corrected criterion with w_{a}\equiv 1 to isolate the effect of weighting the stopping rule for the target policy. All rules choose the smallest minimizing iteration. For cross-validation, a random partition of the complete logged sample defines the folds independently of the observations. We train each arm’s network on the complement of each fold and pool its weighted squared residuals over the held-out observations from that arm. The selected number of steps is then used to fit the model on the full arm sample from the common initialization. Consequently, every stopping rule is evaluated on the same full-data training trajectory. Its selection regret is

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.3\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}})-\min_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g_{\mathbf{t}}).(543)
1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.4

The minimum separates over arms. The reward-noise contribution does not depend on the stopping times, so the same regret is obtained using \mathcal{R}_{\nu}.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.5

For risk estimation in Figures Figure 4 and Figure 6, we compare the criterion with \mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)} in ((561)), including the reward-noise contribution. The reported RMSE is the square root of the mean squared discrepancy, where the mean is taken over arms, candidate iterations, and datasets. Selection regret is reported on the total target-risk scale.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.6

For ten-fold cross-fitting (CF10), we randomly partition the complete logged sample into ten folds independently of the observations. Corrected stopping minimizes ((557)) on each arm’s complete training-complement path. For inner-validation stopping, we split the complement within each arm into 70\% for training and 30\% for selection. These partitions are independent of the contexts and rewards. We select by held-out weighted squared residuals, restart from the common initialization, and refit on the complete arm-specific complement. Both procedures use the same folds and candidate iterations, exclude the evaluation fold from fitting and selection, and average ordinary held-out DR scores with augmentation coefficient one.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.7

The inverse propensity scoring (IPS) and self-normalized inverse propensity scoring (SNIPS) estimators use the same logged sample:

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.8\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{IPS}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})R_{i},\qquad\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{SNIPS}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})R_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})}.(544)
1.1.1/1.1.16/1.3.9

For the direct comparison of the Onsager correction, we evaluate the DR estimator in ((427)) and ADR at identical full-data models and stopping times. We likewise compare ADM with the unadjusted empirical average of the same fitted predictions. The target in this latter comparison is \mathcal{V}_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu), evaluated separately for each fitted model.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.4.1

J.3 Vanishing-fraction holdouts

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.4.2

We compare two holdout sizes fixed before running the experiment, h=\lceil\sqrt{m}\rceil and h=\lceil m^{2/3}\rceil, on the same five Gaussian, uniform-logging settings and 200 datasets per dimension as Figure Figure 4. Both satisfy h\to\infty and h/m\to 0. For each dataset, one permutation independent of the observations defines nested holdouts of these sizes. Each arm’s network is trained on its complement from the common initialization. We average weighted squared residuals over that arm’s held-out observations and select the smallest minimizing iteration. The selected iteration is then evaluated on the same full-data trajectory as the other stopping rules, corresponding to full-data refitting.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.4.3

Table Table 1 reports the risk-estimation RMSE and selection regret defined in Appendix §1.3. Both holdouts have larger errors and regret than the corrected criterion and ten-fold CV at every dimension. For both metrics, all paired pointwise 95\% intervals favor the corrected criterion and CV over the holdouts; risk-estimation comparisons use MSE. Intervals use within-dataset differences, as described in Appendix §1.10. The two schedules thus show a finite-sample accuracy–cost trade-off: correction is more accurate, while the holdouts are cheaper (Appendix §1.12); their asymptotic comparison remains open.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.5.1

J.4 Target-policy weighting

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.5.2

Figure Figure 7 uses three arms with reward links \varphi_{1}^{\ast}(y)=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tanh(y)+\tfrac{1}{2}\tanh^{2}(y), \varphi_{2}^{\ast}(y)=-\tfrac{1}{2}+\tanh(2y)-\tfrac{1}{2}\tanh^{2}(y), and \varphi_{3}^{\ast}(y)=\tfrac{1}{4}+\cos(y). Writing z=(\beta_{1}^{\top}x,\beta_{2}^{\top}x,\beta_{3}^{\top}x), the four policies are uniform, \operatorname{softmax}(2z), \operatorname{softmax}(-2z), and \operatorname{softmax}(2(z_{2},z_{3},z_{1})). We use m=3d at d\in\{128,256,512\}, with 200 datasets per dimension and the network and training schedule above. Every policy uses the same logged datasets, training trajectories, and Onsager correction, so the comparison changes only the weights used for selection.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.5.3

Averaging within each dataset over the three nonuniform policies, weighting reduces prediction risk relative to unweighted corrected selection by 0.0315, 0.0311, and 0.0327 across the three dimensions. The corresponding reductions relative to weighted ten-fold CV are 0.0281, 0.0267, and 0.0293. Weighting reduces risk for \operatorname{softmax}(2z) and \operatorname{softmax}(-2z) at every dimension, with the larger reduction for the former. For the uniform policy, weighted and unweighted selection coincide. For the cyclically permuted policy, paired intervals for weighted versus unweighted selection contain zero at all three dimensions. The corrected weighted rule has lower mean regret than weighted CV in every policy–dimension setting; its paired interval excludes zero except for \operatorname{softmax}(2z) at d=128.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.6.1

J.5 Value estimation at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.6.2

We use the five m=2d settings of Figure Figure 9, with the fitting and selection protocols in Appendix §1.3. To compare the selected complement-trained models, we compute their target-policy prediction errors on independent test contexts, conditional on each training complement, and average across folds using held-out fold sizes, using the numerical references in Appendix §1.10.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.6.4

For the bias–variance decomposition, let e_{r} be a procedure’s policy-value error on dataset r, with B=200 datasets, and let \bar{e}=B^{-1}\sum_{r}e_{r}. We report empirical squared bias \bar{e}^{2}, variance B^{-1}\sum_{r}(e_{r}-\bar{e})^{2}, and MSE B^{-1}\sum_{r}e_{r}^{2}. The first two sum exactly to the third before rounding. The variance uses denominator B and measures variation across complete value estimates with the initializations fixed. Table Table 3 reports these components and Student t intervals for the mean squared error; the intervals quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty across datasets.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.6.6

The bias intervals for ADR and both CF10 procedures contain zero at every dimension. Paired 95\% MSE intervals favor ADR over corrected-stopping CF10 at d=256 and over inner-validation CF10 at d=256,2048; the remaining intervals contain zero. Corrected stopping lowers CF10’s MSE point estimate at every dimension, with a paired interval excluding zero only at d=2048. Prediction-risk improvements need not translate proportionally into value-MSE gains: DR variance combines errors across arms, and cross-fitted estimates also include covariance between folds.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.6.7

ADR has lower MSE than IPS at d=256,512,2048 and than SNIPS at d=2048, with paired 95\% intervals below zero. The remaining intervals contain zero. These comparisons measure finite-sample MSE: with known logging, IPS is unbiased and consistent under the stated moment conditions.

J.6 Risk curves and leave-one-out refitting

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.7.2

Figure Figure 2 shows the two-arm risk curves at d=512 and m=1024. In later iterations, the training-residual criterion decreases while the test risk rises; the corrected criterion follows the test risk.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.7.4

All layers are retrained from the same initialization and with the same learning rates, retaining the original arm denominator N_{a} in the loss. The discrepancy is the root mean squared prediction difference over these rows and datasets.

Figure Figure 3 shows this discrepancy along training. At t=30, the corrected prediction’s root mean squared discrepancy decreases from 0.177 to 0.086 as d increases from 128 to 512, while the unadjusted prediction’s discrepancy remains near 1.17.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.8.1

J.7 Nonuniform logging

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.8.2

We repeat the two-arm Gaussian experiment with context-independent logging probabilities \mu(1)\in\{0.5,0.25,0.1\} and \mu(2)=1-\mu(1). We use d\in\{512,1024,2048\} and m=2d, with 200 independent datasets at each setting. The reward links, target policy, initial weights, network architecture, and training schedule remain as specified above, with \eta=2. The uniform-logging reference uses new datasets generated for this comparison.

1.1.1/1.1.16/1.8.3

Each arm’s criterion uses w_{a}(X)=\nu(a\mid X)/\mu(a). We measure error in estimating total target-policy test risk by comparing \sum_{a=1}^{2}\mu(a)\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t_{a})} with \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\mathbf{t}}), and form the corresponding comparisons for training residuals and cross-validation. The reported RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error over all 31\times 31 pairs of stopping times and datasets. This differs from the arm-wise RMSE in Figure Figure 4. Figure Figure 5 shows that the corrected criterion’s total-risk RMSE and mean selection regret decrease with dimension under each logging distribution.
