1.1.1/1.1.2/1.1.1

2 Statistical Framework

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.1

2.1 Problem Formulation

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.10

Although g^{\ast} is unknown, the zero-mean independent noise assumption gives \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g)=\mathbb{E}[w_{A}(X)\varepsilon^{2}]+\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g). The noise term does not depend on g, so minimizing test risk also minimizes prediction error over the same candidate models.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.11

Our goal is to construct a model selector based on \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g) and to use the selected reward model for policy value estimation, without sample splitting. Note that for learned predictors, all risk and value functionals are understood to be for an independent test draw, conditional on the training data and network initializations; these are defined formally in Appendix §1.1.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.12

Doubly robust value estimation.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.13

For a reward model g, the doubly robust score is defined as

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.14\psi_{g}(X,A,R)\coloneqq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\mid X)g(X,a)+w_{A}(X)\{R-g(X,A)\}.(545)
1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.15

Let P_{d} denote expectation over a new observation Q=(X,A,R) from the logging distribution, holding the reward model fixed; the subscript allows the data law to depend on dimension d. For any fixed g satisfying \mathbb{E}[\sum_{a}\nu(a\mid X)|g(X,a)|]<\infty, and assuming \mathbb{E}[w_{A}(X)|R|]<\infty, conditioning on X yields

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.16\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\psi_{g}(X,A,R)\mid X](546)
1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.17

Because the logging probabilities are known, P_{d}\psi_{g}=\mathcal{V}(\nu) for every fixed reward model, even when g\neq g^{\ast} (setting g=0 gives the inverse propensity scoring, or IPS, score). The identity also holds for a fitted model, provided the evaluation data is independent of the data used for fitting and selection.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.18

Cross-fitting avoids the need for an additional evaluation sample by applying this identity on disjoint partitions of the data: each observation is evaluated using a model fitted and selected without its fold, so its score has a conditional mean of \mathcal{V}(\nu) given its training complement ([24]; [4]). Thus, with a fixed number of folds, and under suitable moment bounds ([4]), value estimation is consistent even when prediction error persists.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.19

However, each reward model is consequently trained on a reduced sample, and reward model selection still matters for the precision of value estimation. When an inner validation split selects the model, it assesses models trained on fewer observations than the subsequent refit on the complete training complement. This training-size mismatch can make stopping-time selection suboptimal after refitting (see Appendix §1.1). In Section §1.1, we compare this procedure with our corrected criterion, which selects directly on that complement.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.2

OPE in contextual bandit settings.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.20

An alternative is to reuse the full sample for training, selection, and evaluation and show that the resulting dependence has a negligible effect. Let P_{m,d} be the empirical measure of the logged sample and let \mathbb{G}_{m,d}=\sqrt{m}(P_{m,d}-P_{d}). If \widehat{g} is fitted and selected on this sample, the same-sample DR estimator P_{m,d}\psi_{\widehat{g}} satisfies the exact decomposition

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.21\sqrt{m}\{P_{m,d}\psi_{\widehat{g}}-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\}=\sqrt{m}\{P_{m,d}\psi_{\widehat{g}}-P_{d}\psi_{g^{\ast}}\}=\mathbb{G}_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}}+\mathbb{G}_{m,d}(\psi_{\widehat{g}}-\psi_{g^{\ast}}).(547)
1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.22

The first term is the fluctuation of the score using the true reward function. The second is the empirical-process term that arises due to replacing g^{\ast} with the fitted model \widehat{g}. Note that there is no population remainder because we assume known logging probabilities. If the second term is o_{p}(1), fitting and selecting the model on the same observations as the evaluation data does not change the first-order behavior of estimator P_{m,d}\psi_{\widehat{g}} relative to P_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}} at the \sqrt{m} scale.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.23

For a fixed distribution P, the second term is o_{p}(1) if \psi_{\widehat{g}} belongs with probability tending to one to a fixed P-Donsker class and \|\psi_{\widehat{g}}-\psi_{g^{\ast}}\|_{L^{2}(P)}\to_{p}0 ([17]). Suitable algorithmic stability, together with nuisance convergence and regularity conditions, also permits asymptotically normal estimation without sample splitting ([3]).

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.24

These sufficient conditions are not automatic in our proportional regime. Indeed, prediction error need not vanish, and as we show in Appendix §1.2, even a class of linear reward models with uniformly vanishing L^{2}(P_{d}) score errors can have a nonvanishing empirical-process supremum.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.25

Rather than assuming the effect of sample reuse is negligible at first-order, we analyze the fitted reward models at candidate (for selection) gradient-descent iterates and apply an Onsager correction to their same-sample evaluation. Section §1.3 establishes consistency of our adjusted doubly robust (ADR) estimator (developed in Section §1.3) on the full training sample without requiring prediction error to vanish. It also shows why the correction matters: uncorrected same-sample DR estimation can be inconsistent after a single gradient-descent step.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.3

We observe an i.i.d. sample \mathcal{D}_{m}\coloneqq\{Q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} collected under a context-independent logging policy \mu. Each observation Q_{i}=(X_{i},A_{i},R_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[K]\times\mathbb{R} with K\geq 2 comprises the context, the logged action, and the resulting reward. We assume the standard positivity condition ([7]): \mu(a)\geq c>0 for every a\in[K]. We assume rewards are generated as R_{i}\coloneqq g^{\ast}(X_{i},A_{i})+\varepsilon_{i} with some g^{\ast}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[K]\to\mathbb{R}, where, conditional on A_{i}=a, the noise \varepsilon_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is independent of X_{i}, mean-zero, and has finite variance. We wish to evaluate a fixed target policy \nu, specified independently of the logged sample and allowed to depend on the contexts. Let \nu(a\mid x) denote the probability of choosing action a given context x. The value of the target policy \nu is defined as:

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.4\mathcal{V}(\nu)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{P_{\nu}}[R]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{X}}\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{A\,|\,X}}\mathbb{E}_{P_{R\,|\,A,X}}[R]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X)g^{\ast}(X,a)\right].(548)
1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.5

Here the final expectation is over the marginal distribution of X. To make the dependence on the true reward function explicit, we also write this value as \mathcal{V}_{g^{\ast}}(\nu). For any fixed measurable reward model g:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[K]\to\mathbb{R} satisfying \mathbb{E}[\sum_{a}\nu(a\mid X)|g(X,a)|]<\infty, define \mathcal{V}_{g}(\nu) by replacing g^{\ast} with g in the final expression above. This is the population quantity estimated by the direct method (DM) ([39]; [7]).

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.6

Importance-weighted risk as selection criterion.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.7

Let w_{a}(x):=\nu(a\,|\,x)/\mu(a) be the target-to-logging importance ratio ([29]; [9]) for arm a, and observe that since \nu(\cdot\,|\,x) is a distribution, w_{a}(x)\geq 0 and \sum_{a}\mu(a)w_{a}(x)=1 for all x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We distinguish the reward model’s squared error relative to the true reward function, \mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g), from its squared error in predicting a new reward, \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g). Averaging under the target policy, we define these quantities as

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.8\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X)\left(g(X,a)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\right)^{2},\quad\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[w_{A}(X)\left(R-g(X,A)\right)^{2}\right].(549)
1.1.1/1.1.2/1.2.9

For a single-arm predictor g_{a}, let \mathcal{R}_{\nu,a}^{\circ}(g_{a})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\nu(a\,|\,X)\left(g_{a}(X)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\right)^{2}]. Two facts make \mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g) useful for OPE. First, Cauchy–Schwarz gives \left\lvert\mathcal{V}_{g}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right\rvert^{2}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g), so prediction error bounds the squared error in the model-induced policy value. Second, Proposition 12 uses this prediction error to bound the additional variance of a DR score evaluated on an observation independent of model fitting, relative to the score using g^{\ast}. These bounds motivate prediction risk as a selection objective; minimizing it need not minimize the value estimator’s mean squared error.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.3.1

2.2 Neural Reward Learning

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.3.2

We fit a separate reward model for each arm. For a\in[K], let \mathcal{I}_{a}\coloneqq\{i\in[m]:A_{i}=a\} be the indices of observations assigned to arm a, with count N_{a}\coloneqq|\mathcal{I}_{a}|. Because logging is context-independent, conditioning on the action labels preserves the common context distribution within each arm. Each model is a feed-forward neural network of depth L\geq 2, hidden width q\geq 1, and scalar output. The learnable weight parameter is W_{a}=(W_{a,1},W_{a,[2:L]}), comprising the first layer W_{a,1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q} and the deeper layers W_{a,[2:L]}. The learned predictor is defined by:

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.3.3f_{W_{a}}(x)\coloneqq G_{W_{a,[2:L]}}\bigl(x^{\top}W_{a,1}\bigr),(550)
1.1.1/1.1.2/1.3.4

where G_{W_{a,[2:L]}}:\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R} is the scalar feed-forward map defined by the deeper layers acting on the first-layer hidden state u=x^{\top}W_{a,1}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}. We identify hidden-state rows in \mathbb{R}^{1\times q} with elements of \mathbb{R}^{q} when evaluating the network, and write gradients with respect to these coordinates as column vectors. We use smooth activations throughout. The collection of arm-wise initializations (W_{a}^{(0)})_{a\in[K]} is jointly independent of \mathcal{D}_{m}, with first-layer weights scaled by d^{-1/2}. The prescribed deterministic layer-wise learning-rate schedule is denoted by \{\eta_{a,\alpha}^{(s)}:\alpha\in[1:L],s\geq 0\}, where \alpha indexes network layers. Appendix §1.1 states the architecture, initialization, and regularity conditions, including the representation of the scalar output used to apply the state-evolution results.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.3.5

Simultaneous full-batch gradient descent (GD) on every layer of the arm-wise squared loss

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.3.6\mathcal{L}_{a}(W_{a})\coloneqq(2N_{a})^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}\bigl(R_{i}-f_{W_{a}}(X_{i})\bigr)^{2}(551)
1.1.1/1.1.2/1.3.7

produces iterates \{W_{a}^{(t)}\}_{t\in\mathcal{T}} and fitted arm-wise models g_{a,t}(x)\coloneqq f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(x). For an iterate vector \mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{K})\in\mathcal{T}^{K}, we write g_{\mathbf{t}}(x,a)\coloneqq g_{a,t_{a}}(x).

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.3.8

We analyze this arm-wise reward learning in the high-dimensional proportional regime, where the aspect ratio m/d\to\phi\in(0,\infty) with the number of arms K, network depth L, width q, and nonempty GD iterate grid \mathcal{T}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} all finite and fixed. Unlike neural tangent kernel-type regimes, where representations remain close to initialization during training ([14]; [34]), our finite-width setting allows non-trivial feature learning across multiple layers.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.4.1

2.3 Assumptions

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.4.2

We make the following assumptions for our analysis. Most are standard regularity conditions used in finite-width state-evolution analyses, as in [10]; we emphasize the assumptions that concern the OPE problem structure and target-policy weighting. The formal exposition of all conditions in this section, including on the true reward function and neural network architecture, is provided in Appendix §1.1.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.4.3

Assumption 1 (paper: assumption 2.1 (Known context-independent logging under positivity))

The logging policy is known and context-independent, with \mu(a)\geq c>0 for every a\in[K], where c is independent of d.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.4.4

Assumption 2 (paper: assumption 2.2 (Single-index rewards under Gaussian design))

The contexts satisfy X_{i}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). For each arm a, assume g^{\ast}(x,a)=\varphi_{a}^{\ast}(\beta_{a}^{\top}x) with \left\|\beta_{a}\right\|_{2}=1, \sqrt{d}\left\|\beta_{a}\right\|_{\infty}=d^{o(1)}, and \varphi_{a}^{\ast} smooth and of polynomial growth. We also let the arm-wise noise \varepsilon_{i}\,|\,A_{i}=a be sub-Gaussian with a dimension-independent parameter.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.4.5

Assumption 3 (paper: assumption 2.3 (Multi-index importance weights))

We let w_{a} be a multi-index function, i.e., w_{a}(x)=h_{a}(\Upsilon^{\top}x) with \Upsilon=(\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{\ell})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times\ell}, \Upsilon^{\top}\Upsilon=I_{\ell}, \sqrt{d}\,\left\|\gamma_{j}\right\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\Upsilon} for each j, and h_{a} is nonnegative, bounded, and Lipschitz, with \sum_{a}\mu(a)h_{a}(u)=1 for every u\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}, for some fixed \ell\geq 1. The coordinate bound and the common boundedness and Lipschitz constants are independent of d.

1.1.1/1.1.2/1.4.6

Assumption Assumption 1 accommodates practically relevant logging policies such as pure exploration, randomized controlled trials and A/B tests. Our guarantees assume known logging probabilities. Under the proportional regime, this assumption ensures that the arm-wise aspect ratios \phi_{a}=N_{a}/d belong to a fixed interval [c_{-},c_{+}]\subset(0,\infty) with probability tending to one. Proposition Proposition 1 yields this count bound and the resulting reduction to arm-wise regression. Assumption Assumption 2 permits unknown nonlinear, arm-specific link functions—a setting of active interest in recent bandit literature ([16]; [18]; [12]). The isotropic Gaussian design is a standard, if restrictive, assumption in state evolution theory ([36]; [38]; [37]); extensions of the weighted comparison beyond Gaussian contexts are discussed in Section §1.1. Finally, sub-Gaussian noise is assumed merely for convenience; our proofs hold under milder moment and envelope conditions detailed in Appendix §1.1. Assumption Assumption 3 includes e.g. logistic, softmax, and probit policies whose scores depend on a fixed number of linear projections satisfying the stated bounds. Different arms may use different projections, provided their joint span admits an orthonormal basis \Upsilon satisfying the coordinate bounds above. For isotropic Gaussian contexts, Corollary Corollary 4 permits arbitrary fixed reward and policy-index directions, including axis-aligned directions, under the stated data-independent initialization and size conditions.

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.1.1

3 Full-Sample OPE via Onsager Correction

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.1.2

This section introduces our full-sample OPE procedure based on the general first-order method (GFOM) Onsager correction ([36]; [2]; [11]; [10]). We first correct each training observation’s hidden state to account for its contribution to the fitted weights, removing the leading sample-reuse bias induced by gradient-based training. We then use the resulting predictions for model selection and for direct and doubly robust value estimation, without sample splitting.

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.2.1

3.1 GFOM-Corrected Hidden States

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.2.2

Our goal is to estimate the weighted test risk \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g) ((549)) without a holdout set. We apply the GFOM correction separately to each arm’s fitted network. Fix an arm a, and let X_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{a}\times d} be its design matrix. At iterate t, the first-layer pre-activation on training observation i is \widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(t)}=X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)} for i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}. To estimate test error from the training residuals, we account for observation i’s influence on the gradient updates that produced W_{a,1}^{(t)}. The neural Onsager correction of [10] removes the leading self-interaction by adding a term to the hidden state. To define it, for each step r, let

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.2.3\Psi_{i,a}^{(r)}\coloneqq\left(G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(r)}}(\widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(r)})-R_{i}\right)\nabla_{u}G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(r)}}(\widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(r)})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times q},(552)
1.1.1/1.1.3/1.2.4

and let \widetilde{U}_{a}^{(r)} and \Psi_{a}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{a}\times q} collect the corresponding rows.

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.2.5

Thus, each row’s \Psi_{i,a}^{(r)} is the gradient of (one half of) the squared residual with respect to the first-layer pre-activation, written as a row vector, so the first-layer loss gradient is N_{a}^{-1}X_{a}^{\top}\Psi_{a}^{(r)}. From this training trajectory, the recursion detailed in Appendix §1.1 computes the Onsager matrices \widehat{\rho}_{a,t,s}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}, s=1,\ldots,t.

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.2.6

The GFOM-corrected hidden state is then defined as follows. We set \widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(0)}=\widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(0)} at initialization. At each subsequent iterate, the corrected hidden state for i\in\mathcal{I}_{a} is

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.2.7\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)}=X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)}+\phi_{a}^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\eta_{a,1}^{(s-1)}\Psi_{i,a}^{(s-1)}\widehat{\rho}_{a,t,s}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times q}.(553)
1.1.1/1.1.3/1.2.8

Let \widehat{U}_{a}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{a}\times q} collect these rows. It is computed from the same arm-wise training trajectory and does not require sample splitting, leave-one-out retraining, or knowledge of the true reward function.

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.1

3.2 Model Selection and Value Estimation without Sample Splitting

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.10

Fix an iterate vector \mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}. For observation i, the model for action A_{i} was trained using that observation, so we evaluate it with the corrected hidden state. The models for the other actions were trained on disjoint observations, so we use their fitted predictions without correction. Define

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.11\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{t}}(X_{i},a)\coloneqq\begin{cases}G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t_{a})}}(\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t_{a})}),&a=A_{i},\\ G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t_{a})}}(X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t_{a})}),&a\neq A_{i}.\end{cases}(554)
1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.12

The adjusted direct method (ADM) value estimator is

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.13\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})\coloneqq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\,|\,X_{i})\,\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{t}}(X_{i},a),(555)
1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.14

and the adjusted doubly robust (ADR) value estimator is

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.15\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})\coloneqq\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})+\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{A_{i}}(X_{i})\left(R_{i}-\widehat{g}_{\mathbf{t}}(X_{i},A_{i})\right).(556)
1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.16

The two procedures use the same corrected hidden states but target different quantities. The selection criterion estimates target-policy-weighted test risk. ADM estimates the fitted-model value, while ADR estimates the true policy value. Section §1.1 establishes consistency uniformly over the candidate iterations, without sample splitting. For a new context x, we use the selected network g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}}(x,a); the adjustment in ((554)) is used only to evaluate observations included in that arm’s training sample.

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.2

The corrected hidden states ((553)) are used to select the gradient-descent stopping iterate and estimate the target-policy value from the training sample only.

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.3

Model selection.

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.4

For each arm a and each iterate t\in\mathcal{T}, we define the corrected weighted residual criterion

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.5\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}w_{a}(X_{i})\left(R_{i}-G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}(\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)})\right)^{2}.(557)
1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.6

The criterion replaces each fitted prediction in the importance-weighted average of squared training residuals with a prediction based on the corrected hidden state. Theorem Theorem 1 proves that it consistently estimates the fitted network’s weighted test risk, including the reward-noise contribution. We select the stopping iterate by minimizing this criterion:

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.7\displaystyle\hat{t}_{a}\in\arg\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)},(558)
1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.8

breaking ties using a fixed ordering of \mathcal{T}. The selected iterate vector for the arms is therefore \hat{\mathbf{t}}=(\hat{t}_{1},\ldots,\hat{t}_{K}).

1.1.1/1.1.3/1.3.9

Value estimation.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.1.1

4 Theoretical Guarantees

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.1.2

We first show that our in-sample selection criterion ((557)) uniformly estimates conditional arm-wise weighted test risk, enabling near-oracle early stopping (Section §1.2). We then establish consistency of ADM for the model-induced value and of ADR for the true policy value, contrast these guarantees with a one-step inconsistency example for uncorrected DR, and bound the conditional variance of a DR score evaluated on an independent observation (Section §1.3). Finally, we outline the proof strategy (Section §1.4). All results assume the statistical framework of §1.1 and the formal regularity conditions in Appendix §1.1.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.1

4.1 Consistent Risk Estimation and Near-Oracle Model Selection

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.10\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}})(559)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.11\displaystyle\left|\mathcal{V}_{g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right|^{2}(560)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.12

The weighted test risk \mathcal{R}_{\nu} is the sum of the weighted prediction error \mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ} and a noise term that does not depend on the fitted model. The bound on total test risk therefore also holds for \mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}. Since \mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ}(g) bounds |\mathcal{V}_{g}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)|^{2}, as shown in Section §1.2, this gives the stated bound on the fitted model’s policy value error. Thus, without sample splitting, the selected models attain the smallest prediction risk among the candidate iterates up to o_{p}(1).

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.2

For each arm a, let Z_{a}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and let \xi_{a}^{\mathrm{new}} have the law of \varepsilon_{i}\mid A_{i}=a. These draws are independent of each other and of the training sample and network initializations. The weighted test risk at iterate t, conditional on the training data and initializations, is

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.3\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\!\left[w_{a}(Z_{a})\left(\varphi_{a}^{\ast}(\beta_{a}^{\top}Z_{a})+\xi_{a}^{\mathrm{new}}-f_{W_{a}^{(t)}}(Z_{a})\right)^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}\right],(561)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.4

where \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}} is generated by the training sample and all network initializations. The total test risk is \mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\mathbf{t}})=\sum_{a}\mu(a)\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t_{a})} almost surely. The following theorem shows that the criterion consistently estimates each arm’s conditional test risk, uniformly over t\in\mathcal{T}.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.5

Theorem 1 (paper: theorem 4.1 (Uniform consistency))

Assume the statistical framework of Section §1.1 and the formal conditions in Appendix §1.1. For every arm a\in[K], as N_{a},d\to\infty with \phi_{a} bounded away from zero and infinity, the criterion in ((557)) and the conditional risk in ((561)) satisfy

\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0. (562)

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.6\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)}-\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0.(562)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.7

This uniform consistency yields the following guarantee for the stopping rule \hat{t}_{a} in ((558)). The proof is given in Appendix §1.4.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.8

Theorem 2 (paper: theorem 4.2 (Arm-wise iterate selection and oracle inequality))

Under the assumptions and asymptotic regime of Theorem Theorem 1, the selector in ((558)) satisfies, for every a\in[K],

\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(\hat{t}_{a})}\leq\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}+o_{p}(1). (563)

Moreover,

\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\nu}(g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}})

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.2.9\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(\hat{t}_{a})}\leq\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{E}_{a,\mathrm{ind}}^{(t)}+o_{p}(1).(563)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.1

4.2 Consistency of Value Estimation

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.10

Proposition 14 (paper: proposition 4.3 (Inconsistency after one gradient-descent step))

For the constant-reward example in Section §1.3, assume the conditions of Theorem Theorem 1, 1\in\mathcal{T}, and m/d\to\phi\in(0,\infty). Then

\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(1,\ldots,1)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\xrightarrow{p}-\frac{\eta c(K-1)}{\phi}. (564)

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.11\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(1,\ldots,1)-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\xrightarrow{p}-\frac{\eta c(K-1)}{\phi}.(564)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.12

The limit is nonzero because c\neq 0, \eta>0, and K\geq 2. Thus, the DR estimator is inconsistent at the fixed first GD iterate. Appendix §1.2 gives the proof and also characterizes the error of \widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}} uniformly over the candidate iterations, including choices made from the training data.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.13

Consistency of ADM and ADR.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.14

Correcting the training predictions yields the following guarantees for ADM ((555)) and ADR ((556)). ADM targets the population value induced by the learned reward model, while ADR targets the true policy value \mathcal{V}(\nu) ((548)). The proof is in Appendix §1.1.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.15

Theorem 3 (paper: theorem 4.4 (Uniform consistency of value estimation))

Under the assumptions and asymptotic regime of Theorem Theorem 1, the estimators in ((555)) and ((556)) satisfy

\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(\nu)\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0,\qquad\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0. (565)

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.16\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(\nu)\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0,\qquad\sup_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{K}}\left\lvert\widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{ADR}}(\mathbf{t})-\mathcal{V}(\nu)\right\rvert\xrightarrow{p}0.(565)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.17

Both conclusions hold for any choice \widehat{\mathbf{t}}\in\mathcal{T}^{K} based on the training data and initializations, including the rule in ((558)). ADR remains consistent when the selected model’s prediction error does not converge to zero. ADM estimates the value induced by that model, so ADM minus ADR consistently estimates \mathcal{V}_{g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu)-\mathcal{V}(\nu), as formalized in Corollary 1.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.18

Variance of a DR score on an independent observation.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.19

We now return to the role of prediction risk in controlling the variance of the score \psi_{g}(X,A,R) in ((545)), evaluated on an observation independent of the training sample and initializations. Conditional on \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, the fitted model is fixed. Define the weighted prediction error

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.2

ADM and ADR consistently estimate their respective values using the full training sample. A single gradient-descent step example first shows why the population identity P_{d}\psi_{g}=\mathcal{V}(\nu) alone does not ensure consistency of uncorrected same-sample DR.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.20\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}}(g)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\nu(a\mid X)\frac{1-\mu(a)}{\mu(a)}\{g(X,a)-g^{\ast}(X,a)\}^{2}\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}\right].(566)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.21

By the variance decomposition in Proposition 12, \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}}(g) bounds the increase in this conditional variance relative to the score using the true reward function g^{\ast}. To state the consequence for model selection, define

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.22\displaystyle c_{-}(\mu)(567)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.23

Applying Theorem Theorem 2 separately to each arm and weighting its regret by (1-\mu(a))/\mu(a) gives the following bound.

Under the assumptions and asymptotic regime of Theorem Theorem 2, let \hat{\mathbf{t}} be selected by ((558)). For an observation (X,A,R) independent of \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, and with \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DR}} and the constants defined in ((566)) and ((567)),

The proof is given in Appendix §1.3. The corollary holds the selected model g_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}} fixed and bounds the variance of its DR score ((545)) on a fresh observation. ADR in ((556)) averages corrected scores on the training sample. Its sampling variance also depends on covariances between these scores, which share fitted models and correction terms. Characterizing these joint fluctuations is left to future work.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.3

Inconsistency of DR evaluation on the training sample.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.30

We also note here that the cross-fitted value estimator requires a separate variance analysis in the proportional regime. Its standard \sqrt{m}-convergence to P_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}} argument uses vanishing fitted-score error, which is a much stronger condition under proportionally growing d. In a related setting with linear outcomes and estimated logistic propensities, [15] characterize variance inflation and cross-fold covariance. This motivates our comparison of ADR both with cross-fitted DR and with the oracle DR benchmark empirically in Section §1.1.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.4

Consider the DR estimator formed by evaluating the fitted models directly on their training observations, \widehat{\mathcal{V}}_{\mathrm{DR}}^{\mathrm{nv}}(\mathbf{t})=m^{-1}\sum_{i}\psi_{g_{\mathbf{t}}}(Q_{i}). Take \nu=\mu and a constant reward R=c almost surely. With \Lambda as in Assumption Assumption 4, fix 0<|c|\leq\Lambda and 0<\eta\leq\Lambda. For each arm, use a network with depth L=2, width q=1, and identity activation \sigma_{1}=\mathrm{id}. Initialize W_{a,1}^{(0)}=0 and W_{a,2}^{(0)}=1, and set the first-layer learning rate to \eta_{a,1}^{(0)}=\eta.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.5

For each observed arm, write \overline{X}_{a}=N_{a}^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}X_{i}. The loss gradients at initialization are

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.6\nabla_{W_{a,1}}\mathcal{L}_{a}(W_{a}^{(0)})=-c\,\overline{X}_{a},\qquad\nabla_{W_{a,2}}\mathcal{L}_{a}(W_{a}^{(0)})=0.(571)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.7

Thus, one simultaneous full-batch GD step produces

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.8g_{a,1}(x)=\eta c\,x^{\top}\overline{X}_{a}.(572)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.3.9

For i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}, the prediction g_{a,1}(X_{i}) contains the term \eta c\|X_{i}\|_{2}^{2}/N_{a}, which is the contribution of observation i to its own fitted prediction. This contribution does not vanish when N_{a} and d grow proportionally. The following proposition yields the resulting policy-value error.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.1

4.3 Proof Strategy and Key Novelty

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.10

The Onsager matrices are those of [10] since the target-policy weights enter evaluation, while training still minimizes the unweighted arm-wise squared loss.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.2

We outline the proof that the corrected criterion consistently estimates conditional test risk. The Onsager correction replaces \widetilde{U}_{i,a}^{(t)} with \widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)} ((553)) to account for observation i’s contribution to its own fitted prediction; see Section §1.2.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.3

State evolution approximates empirical averages along the training trajectory by expectations of functions of a jointly Gaussian sequence. Let \mathfrak{U}_{a}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{q} represent the signal coordinate (\beta_{a}^{\top}X_{i},0,\ldots,0), with zeros added to match the hidden-state dimension, and let \mathfrak{U}_{a}^{(t+1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{q} be the Gaussian vector corresponding to the corrected hidden state at iterate t. The unweighted theory of [10] compares averages of corrected fitted values and squared residuals with expectations under this state evolution.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.4

A key technical challenge is the weighted risk in ((557)), which multiplies each squared residual by w_{a}(X_{i})=h_{a}(\Upsilon^{\top}X_{i}). Consequently, the analysis must track the policy index and learned hidden state jointly, since both depend on X_{i}.

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.5

We account for this dependence by appending a Gaussian vector \mathfrak{U}_{\Upsilon,a}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{\ell}) to the state evolution. The augmented recursion explicitly tracks its covariance with the learned hidden states:

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.6\operatorname{Cov}(\mathfrak{U}_{a}^{(s)},\mathfrak{U}_{\Upsilon,a})=d^{-1/2}D_{a,s-1}^{\top}\Upsilon,(573)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.7

where D_{a,s-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q} is the shift matrix defined by the arm-wise state-evolution recursion. The Gaussian law and covariance above are conditional on \mathcal{G}_{a}, which fixes the action labels, initialization, and realized noise. The recursion and conditioning are specified in Appendix §1.1 and Proposition Proposition 2. The comparison is first established for the auxiliary GFOM and then transferred to the actual corrected states. For example, let V_{a}^{(t)} denote the deeper-layer parameters in the state evolution. The weighted average of corrected predictions satisfies

1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.8\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{a}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{a}}h_{a}(\Upsilon^{\top}X_{i})G_{W_{a,[2:L]}^{(t)}}(\widehat{U}_{i,a}^{(t)})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[h_{a}(\mathfrak{U}_{\Upsilon,a})G_{V_{a}^{(t)}}(\mathfrak{U}_{a}^{(t+1)})\mid\mathcal{G}_{a}\right]+o_{p}(1).(574)
1.1.1/1.1.4/1.4.9

An analogous comparison applies to the weighted squared residual, with the state-evolution expectation averaged over the realized noise values in arm a. These comparisons hold uniformly over the fixed set of candidate iterations. They imply that \widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{a}^{(t)} consistently estimates an intermediate test risk \mathcal{E}_{a,\pi}^{(t)} that uses a new context and a noise value sampled uniformly from the realized training noises (Proposition 4). Proposition 6 then shows that replacing this empirical noise distribution with the true arm-specific noise law changes the risk by o_{p}(1), uniformly over the candidate iterations. This yields consistency for the conditional test risk in ((561)).

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.1

5 Experiments

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.10

The stopping criterion should measure prediction error in the contexts where the target policy uses each arm. To isolate this dependence, we vary the target policy while holding the training data, network trajectories, and Onsager correction fixed. We use three arms and four target policies, with m=3d at d\in\{128,256,512\}. Appendix §1.5 specifies the reward links and policies.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.11

Figure Figure 7 compares the corrected weighted criterion with unweighted selection and target-weighted ten-fold CV. Averaging over the three nonuniform policies at each dimension, weighting reduces the selected model’s prediction risk by 0.031–0.033 relative to unweighted selection. For the uniform policy, the weighted and unweighted rules coincide.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.12

Relative to target-weighted CV, the corrected weighted rule reduces prediction risk by 0.027–0.029, again averaging over the three nonuniform policies at each dimension. Its mean selection regret is lower than CV’s for every policy and dimension. Appendix §1.5 reports the paired comparisons.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.14

Value estimation at the same fitted model.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.15

We next isolate the effect of the value correction. Returning to the two-arm experiment with m=2d, we select the reward model using the corrected criterion and compute DR and ADR from the same fitted networks, stopping times, and logged observations. Figure Figure 8 (left) shows that correction reduces the persistent bias of same-sample DR. At d=2048, the empirical bias magnitude falls by over 95\%, from 0.0149 for DR to 0.0006 for ADR.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.16

To compare precision for the fitted-model value, we also evaluate DM and ADM against the population value induced by their shared fitted model, \mathcal{V}_{g_{\widehat{\mathbf{t}}}}(\nu), computed separately for each dataset. This is the target of the ADM guarantee in Theorem Theorem 3. Cross-arm DM provides an independent-evaluation comparison: it evaluates each selected arm model on contexts logged under the other arm, avoiding reuse of its training observations. ADM reduces MSE relative to cross-arm DM by 50.7\%–57.4\% across the five dimensions, with every paired 95\% interval favoring ADM (Figure Figure 8, right; Appendix §1.3).

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.18

Comparison with cross-fitted DR.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.19

The corrected criterion also improves model selection within ten-fold cross-fitted DR (CF10). Our inner-validation CF10 baseline selects the stopping time on an inner split before refitting on the complete training complement. Selecting directly on that complement with the corrected criterion avoids this additional training-size mismatch while keeping the evaluation fold excluded from fitting and selection. Corrected stopping reduces the complement models’ prediction error by 19.3\%–42.3\% relative to inner validation (Appendix §1.6). We compare both CF10 procedures with ADR, which trains and selects on all available observations for each arm.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.2

In this section, we examine whether the proposed criterion estimates the test risk of the full-data reward model, how its stopping decisions depend on the target policy, and how the correction affects value estimation. We also compare the value estimators’ mean squared errors at both fixed and increasing sample-to-dimension ratios. Experimental details are provided in Appendix §1.1.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.20

Figure Figure 9 shows that ADR has similar observed MSE to corrected-stopping CF10, with substantially lower runtime (Appendix §1.12). At d=2048, their RMSEs are 0.0183 and 0.0185, respectively. ADR has lower MSE point estimates at every dimension, with most paired 95\% intervals including zero. At d=2048, ADR also has lower MSE than IPS and self-normalized IPS (SNIPS), with paired 95\% intervals favoring ADR. Appendix §1.6 reports the paired comparisons and bias–variance decomposition.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.22

Value estimation under increasing sample-to-dimension ratio.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.23

We next examine how the value estimation precision comparison changes as sample size outgrows dimension, using the oracle DR benchmark introduced in Section §1.3. Finally, we examine value estimation as m/d increases, both at fixed d=256 and while dimension grows. Figure Figure 1 reports MSE normalized by \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}/m, the MSE of DR using the true reward function. At the largest sample sizes, ADR and both CF10 procedures have similar MSEs near this oracle benchmark. At (d,m)=(1024,32768), the estimated normalized MSEs of ADR and corrected-stopping CF10 are 1.000 and 1.013, respectively. ADR also has lower MSE than IPS and SNIPS at both endpoints with m=32768. Appendix §1.11 gives the implementation details and paired comparisons.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.24

Across the tested regimes, ADR achieves precision comparable to corrected-stopping CF10, with substantially lower runtime in the matched benchmarks (Appendix §1.12).

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.26

We report the wall-clock runtime for complete ADR, cross-validation, and cross-fitting procedures, including model selection and refitting where required in Appendix §1.12.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.3

Risk estimation and early stopping.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.4

We use a two-arm Gaussian bandit with uniform logging, nonlinear single-index rewards, and a context-dependent target policy. The reward models are sigmoid multilayer perceptrons trained by full-batch gradient descent. We increase d\in\{128,256,512,1024,2048\} with m=2d, using 200 independent datasets per dimension. Appendix §1.1 specifies the data-generating model and training settings.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.5

Figure Figure 4 (left) compares risk estimates against the conditional test risk of the full-data model. Our corrected criterion’s root mean squared error (RMSE) decreases from 0.347 to 0.081, compared with 0.410 to 0.154 for ten-fold cross-validation (CV). At the largest dimension, correction nearly halves CV’s RMSE. Because CV evaluates models trained on fold complements, its discrepancy from full-data risk includes any difference between the test risks of the fold-complement and full-data models. Meanwhile, the importance-weighted mean squared training residuals remain inaccurate across all dimensions, with RMSE between 1.33 and 1.37.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.6

Our corrected criterion also improves stopping decisions (Figure Figure 4, right). We apply each rule’s selected iteration to the same full-data training trajectory. Selection regret is the excess total target-policy prediction risk \mathcal{R}_{\nu}^{\circ} over the best arm-wise stopping times on that trajectory. At d=2048, the corrected rule’s mean regret is 0.0025, less than one-third of CV’s 0.0082, while training-residual stopping has regret near 0.59. Appendix §1.7 provides the risk curves and comparisons with networks retrained after omitting the evaluated observation.

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.7

The selection rule based on the corrected criterion and CV also achieve lower risk-estimation error and selection regret than single holdouts of sizes \lceil\sqrt{m}\rceil and \lceil m^{2/3}\rceil at every tested dimension (Appendix §1.4). These holdouts are faster; Appendix §1.12 reports the computational comparison. Additional experiments with nonuniform logging or non-Gaussian contexts show decreasing corrected risk-estimation error and selection regret as dimension grows. ADR has lower absolute empirical bias than uncorrected DR in these settings (Appendices §1.8 and §1.9).

1.1.1/1.1.5/1.1.9

The role of target-policy weighting.

1.1.1/1.1.6/1.1.1

6 Discussion

1.1.1/1.1.6/1.1.2

We study how to select a reward model trained on the full logged sample and estimate policy value using the same observations. In the proportional regime, our Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion consistently estimates conditional test risk and yields near-oracle stopping among the candidate gradient descent iterates. The correction also enables consistent estimation of the fitted-model value through ADM ((555)) and the true policy value through ADR ((556)), without requiring reward prediction error to vanish.

1.1.1/1.1.6/1.1.3

The experiments in Section §1.1 demonstrate benefits for both full-sample learning and cross-fitting. The corrected criterion improves full-data stopping selection over cross validation and two holdout sample schedules. For estimating the policy value induced by the fitted model, ADM achieves lower RMSE than both (uncorrected) DM on the full sample and cross-arm evaluation. For doubly robust value estimation with 10-fold cross-fitting (CF10), our Onsager-corrected criterion selects directly on each complete training complement and yields reward models with lower mean target-policy-weighted prediction risk than standard inner validation followed by refitting. Full-data ADR achieves comparable observed RMSE to corrected-stopping CF10 at substantially lower runtime.

1.1.1/1.1.6/1.1.4

Note that our experiments (Figure Figure 1) show that ADR and CF10 attain similar MSEs near the oracle DR benchmark as sample size outgrows dimension. These findings motivate for future work a fluctuation theory for ADR that accounts for dependence between its Onsager-corrected scores, as discussed in Section §1.3. Two goals remain: to derive a central limit theorem (CLT) for ADR in the proportional regime and to identify conditions for recovering the same limit as the oracle DR estimator, when d\to\infty with d/m\to 0. For example, showing that ADR differs from P_{m,d}\psi_{g^{\ast}} by o_{p}(m^{-1/2}) would give ADR the same limiting distribution whenever the oracle estimator satisfies a CLT.

1.1.1/1.1.6/1.1.5

Finally, our analysis assumes Gaussian contexts and known context-independent logging. Promising results on experiments with non-Gaussian designs (see Appendix §1.9) motivate extending our weighted state-evolution analysis beyond Gaussian designs. An important next step is also to extend our analysis to context-dependent logging: since it changes the distribution of contexts within each arm’s training sample, it requires a new characterization of the resulting training dynamics and correction.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.1

Appendix A Related Work

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.10

Single-index reward models have been studied for online regret minimization through kernel regression, cross-fitting, and staged exploration [[16], [18], [12]]. Our setting concerns offline evaluation and selection of neural reward models in proportional dimension. Related work constructs risk estimates along gradient-descent trajectories for high-dimensional linear and robust regression [[37], [30]] and develops inference for empirical risk minimization [[11]]. We build directly on [10], who establish state evolution for finite-width neural networks, a computable Onsager correction, consistent estimation of unweighted test error, and early stopping based on that estimate. We retain their correction for the unweighted arm-wise training loss and extend the joint state evolution to include the linear projections that determine the target-policy probabilities. Tracking the covariance between these projections and the learned features gives the weighted risk-estimation and OPE results proved here.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.2

Reward models in off-policy evaluation.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.3

Classic OPE baselines include the direct method (DM) [[39]], inverse propensity scoring (IPS) [[22], [25]], and doubly robust (DR) estimators [[8], [7]]. Subsequent work improves the value estimator’s bias–variance tradeoff through sample-wise interpolation between DR and DM (SWITCH [[33]]), variance-targeted reward modeling (MRDR [[9]]), adaptive blending (CAB [[28]]), and smooth importance-weight corrections (DRos [[26]] and IPS-\lambda/DR-\lambda [[20]]). Our criterion estimates the target-policy-weighted test risk of a neural reward model fitted on the full sample. The corresponding prediction error bounds the squared difference between the model-induced and true policy values, and the additional variance of a DR score evaluated on independent observations.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.4

Semiparametric estimation and sample reuse.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.5

The same-sample empirical-process term in ((547)) is standard in semiparametric analysis [[17]]. When the data distribution is fixed, stochastic equicontinuity of a Donsker empirical process and L^{2} convergence of the fitted score to the score using the true reward function make this term o_{p}(1). Cross-fitting uses independent evaluation observations for each nuisance fit [[24], [4]]; own-observation effects and cross-fitting also appear in series-based semiparametric estimation [[21]]. Stability conditions permit inference without splitting for suitable learners [[3]]. Our correction establishes risk and value consistency along a neural training trajectory in proportional dimension. In this regime, [15] find variance inflation and non-negligible cross-fold covariance for cross-fitted DR with linear outcomes and logistic propensities. These findings motivate future work in studying ADR’s limiting distribution and asymptotic variance, the analysis of which must account for dependence among its corrected scores.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.6

Value estimator selection and reward-model selection.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.7

Several OPE methods select the value estimator or its hyperparameters. SLOPE [[27], [31]] tunes parameters that control the value estimator’s bias–variance tradeoff, while PAS-IF [[32]] selects value estimators using pseudo-evaluation policies. Cross-validated OPE also selects value estimators and their hyperparameters [[5]]. [19] study ridge-based estimation of expected conditional covariance under proportional asymptotics. Prediction-optimal nuisance tuning need not minimize the estimator’s asymptotic variance. Our selector targets weighted test risk; the corresponding prediction risk bounds the additional variance under independent DR evaluation. A held-out importance-weighted residual criterion estimates weighted test risk for a model trained on the complementary sample [[29]]. Cross-validation followed by full-data refitting is therefore a natural comparison for our stopping rule.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.8

Cross-fitting likewise uses models trained on fewer observations than the full-data fit. Within each fold’s training sample, one may use a further validation split to select a stopping iterate and then refit on that training sample. The validation criterion then estimates the risk of the models before refitting, while DR evaluation on the excluded fold uses the refitted model. Our Onsager-corrected criterion can select directly on the complete training complement, while the excluded fold remains independent for DR evaluation; Appendix §1.6 examines this use.

1.1.1/1.1.7/1.1.9

Reward modeling and neural state evolution.

1.1.1/1.1.8/1.1.1

Implementation and complexity.

1.1.1/1.1.8/1.1.31

The algorithm reuses the leading solution and Onsager blocks from the preceding iteration. Computing the new block rows at iteration t costs O(N_{a}q^{3}t^{2}) operations for one arm, and all T iterations cost

1.1.1/1.1.8/1.1.32\sum_{t=1}^{T}O(N_{a}q^{3}t^{2})=O(N_{a}q^{3}T^{3}).(585)
1.1.1/1.1.8/1.1.33

At the final iteration, each row cache has T^{2} blocks of size q\times q, so the block cache stores O(N_{a}T^{2}q^{2}) numbers. Computing the local derivatives adds O(N_{a}Lq^{3}T) operations. For fixed L, this cost remains within the correction bound. These costs are additional to full-batch training, whose first-layer operations cost O(N_{a}dqT). End-to-end storage includes O(N_{a}d) for the design and O(dqT) for the first-layer parameter trajectory, in addition to the correction cache and lower-order fixed-width arrays. Thus, when d\asymp N_{a} and K,L,q,T are fixed, the correction preserves the leading asymptotic dependence on sample size. Its finite-sample overhead can be substantial.

Proof.

The feed-forward and back-propagation maps are independent of the response link. Differentiating the squared loss gives the same gradient identity with \bm{\varphi} in place of the scalar entrywise link. Moreover,

D\bm{\varphi}(w)=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\varphi_{1}^{\prime}(w_{1}),\ldots,\varphi_{q}^{\prime}(w_{q})\bigr). (620)

For j=1,2,3 and v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{q},

[D^{j}\bm{\varphi}(w)[v_{1},\ldots,v_{j}]]_{b}=\varphi_{b}^{(j)}(w_{b})\prod_{h=1}^{j}(v_{h})_{b},\qquad b\in[q]. (621)

Thus, all mixed partial derivatives vanish. With operator norms on the multilinear derivatives, and with D^{0}\bm{\varphi}=\bm{\varphi} measured in the Euclidean norm,

\displaystyle\|D^{j}\bm{\varphi}(w)\|

The second bound follows by integrating the next derivative along the segment from w to w^{\prime}. These are the polynomial-growth and local-Lipschitz bounds used in the HI25 residual, pre-gradient, and derivative estimates.

To make the derivative bounds explicit, let \mathscr{G}_{V}(u) denote the network output as a function of its first-layer hidden state, with the deeper weights V fixed. In column-vector notation its loss gradient is

\displaystyle\mathfrak{S}_{k}(u,w;V)

The activation assumptions and the bounds above imply

\displaystyle\|D^{j}\mathfrak{S}_{k}(u,w;V)\|

For j=0,1,2, the corresponding difference bound is

\displaystyle\|D^{j}\mathfrak{S}_{k}(u,w;V)-D^{j}\mathfrak{S}_{k}(u^{\prime},w^{\prime};V^{\prime})\|

Here the derivatives D^{j} are with respect to (u,w), and the second bound follows by the product rule and integration along the segment joining the two arguments, including their deeper weights. In particular, a change in D\bm{\varphi}(w) is controlled by \|w-w^{\prime}\|.

Each auxiliary output row depends only on the corresponding input rows. The generic GFOM theorems allow these maps to vary across rows and coordinates. Lemma 3 applies these theorems to smooth input cutoffs and removes the cutoffs using polynomial moment bounds. The deterministic gradient-descent comparison uses the loss gradient identity and the value bounds above. For the Onsager comparison, the finite polynomial expansion of the block inverse is controlled by the sum of the two state envelopes, as verified in Lemma 4. These arguments preserve every other hypothesis and give the stated componentwise-link conclusions.

\kappa_{0,d}\coloneqq 1+\max_{a\in[K]}\left\{\|\xi_{\mathcal{I}_{a}}\|_{\infty}+\|\sqrt{d}\,W_{a,1}^{(0)}\|_{\infty}+\max_{\alpha\in[2:L]}\|W_{a,\alpha}^{(0)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\right\}=d^{o_{p}(1)}. (631)

Then, the conclusions of Theorem 1, Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 hold for arbitrary fixed orientations of the reward and policy-index directions.

1.1.1/1.1.9/1.1.86\kappa_{0,d}\coloneqq 1+\max_{a\in[K]}\left\{\|\xi_{\mathcal{I}_{a}}\|_{\infty}+\|\sqrt{d}\,W_{a,1}^{(0)}\|_{\infty}+\max_{\alpha\in[2:L]}\|W_{a,\alpha}^{(0)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\right\}=d^{o_{p}(1)}.(631)
1.1.1/1.1.9/1.1.87

Proof.

Condition on \mathcal{W}^{(0)} and let

S=\operatorname{span}\{\beta_{a},\gamma_{j},(W_{a,1}^{(0)})_{\cdot k}:a\in[K],j\in[\ell],k\in[q]\},\qquad r=\dim S\leq K+\ell+Kq. (632)

Choose an orthonormal basis B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} of S measurably in \mathcal{W}^{(0)}, for example by Gram–Schmidt applied in a fixed order and omitting dependent columns. Let C\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} consist of the first r columns of the real discrete cosine transform, so that C^{\top}C=I_{r} and \max_{i,j}|C_{ij}|\leq\sqrt{2/d}. Completing both frames to orthonormal bases by the same measurable procedure gives an orthogonal matrix Q with Q^{\top}B=C. Thus, Q depends only on the initialization and fixed directions. For v\in S,

\sqrt{d}\,\|Q^{\top}v\|_{\infty}=\sqrt{d}\,\|CB^{\top}v\|_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{2}\,\|B^{\top}v\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{2r}\,\|v\|. (633)

Apply this rotation jointly to the contexts and first-layer parameters:

X_{i}^{\prime}=Q^{\top}X_{i},\qquad\beta_{a}^{\prime}=Q^{\top}\beta_{a},\qquad\Upsilon^{\prime}=Q^{\top}\Upsilon,\qquad W_{a,1}^{\prime}{}^{(0)}=Q^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(0)}. (634)

Leave actions, rewards, noise, and deeper-layer initializations unchanged. Conditional on \mathcal{W}^{(0)}, the rotated contexts remain i.i.d. N(0,I_{d}), independent of the actions and arm-specific noises. The signal and policy directions satisfy their required coordinate bounds with constant \sqrt{2(K+\ell+Kq)}. For each initial first-layer column,

\|(W_{a,1}^{(0)})_{\cdot k}\|\leq\|\sqrt{d}\,W_{a,1}^{(0)}\|_{\infty}. (635)

Consequently the rotated envelope satisfies \max_{a}\varkappa_{\ast,a}^{\prime}\leq C_{0}\kappa_{0,d}=d^{o_{p}(1)} for a constant C_{0} depending only on K,\ell,q.

The conditional comparison arguments apply with all original initializations retained in the conditioning fields. In particular, condition on \mathcal{W}^{(0)}, the action labels, and the noises in an arm. The rotated directions and parameters are then fixed, and that arm’s context rows are still independent standard Gaussians. The bounds in Lemma 5 and Proposition 2 are uniform in these fixed directions and initializations once their coordinate bounds and envelope are specified. Their error bounds are polynomial in \varkappa_{\ast,a}^{\prime}\log d times a negative power of d, so they vanish in probability under ((631)). Conditional probability bounds may be truncated at one before averaging over the initialization and noise. The empirical noise moments are unchanged by rotation. Conditioning additionally on all initializations also preserves the independence used when predictions are evaluated on another arm’s observations. Thus, the risk and value consistency proofs apply to the rotated system, as does the finite-grid selection argument.

It remains to identify their conclusions with the original quantities. Induction in the simultaneous gradient updates gives

W_{a,1}^{\prime}{}^{(t)}=Q^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)},\qquad W_{a,\alpha}^{\prime}{}^{(t)}=W_{a,\alpha}^{(t)}\quad(\alpha\geq 2). (636)

Indeed, X_{i}^{\prime}{}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{\prime}{}^{(t)}=X_{i}^{\top}W_{a,1}^{(t)}, so hidden states and deeper-layer gradients agree, and the first-layer gradient is multiplied by Q^{\top}. The signal and policy indices, hidden-state Hessians, estimated Onsager coefficients, and corrected predictions therefore agree. Hence, the criteria, selected iterations under the same tie rule, and value estimators agree pathwise.

Keep the original initialization in the rotated training field:

\sigma(\mathcal{W}^{(0)},(X_{i}^{\prime},A_{i},R_{i})_{i\in[m]})=\sigma(\mathcal{W}^{(0)},\mathcal{D}_{m})=\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}. (637)

This equality holds because Q is measurable in the retained initialization and the transformation of contexts is invertible given it; it does not require recovering the original initialization from its rotated weights. For a new Gaussian context Z independent of \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{tr}}, let Z^{\prime}=Q^{\top}Z. Its conditional law is still N(0,I_{d}), and predictions, policy weights, and reward means agree at the coupled contexts. Conditional test risks and fitted-model values are therefore equal. This proves the stated conclusions. ∎

□
